projectTitle: Thornridge Insurance: A Migration That Actually Gets Tested, Start to Finish
projectTagline: A 20-video, start-to-finish migration of a production insurance database to Azure SQL Database — security, geo-replication, performance, and automation — for one fictional insurer, from a near-miss disk failure to a database that's secured, documented, and genuinely tested, not just configured.
businessContext:
**Thornridge Insurance** is a fictional mid-size regional insurance company whose core policy and claims database has run on an aging on-premises SQL Server for over 13 years. A recent disk failure came within hours of causing real data loss — backups happened to be current, but it was a close call that finally got leadership to fund a real migration. You've been brought in as an Azure Database Engineer to move the database to Azure SQL Database and build it right this time: real security hardening, real tested high availability and disaster recovery, a real performance baseline, and real automated maintenance — none of which the on-prem server ever had.

This series follows that migration end to end — including a real incident where a long-planned failover drill finally ran and immediately exposed a gap nobody had caught: the application's own connection string was never updated to use the failover group's listener, so even though Azure failed the database over correctly, the app couldn't follow. Found, fixed, and followed by a real recurring drill schedule.
architectureSummary: By the end of this series, Thornridge Insurance has: its policy/claims database migrated from on-premises SQL Server to Azure SQL Database (`thornridge-sql-server`/`PolicyClaimsDB`) via a Data Factory pipeline with a watermark-and-change-tracking incremental sync; real security hardening (Transparent Data Encryption confirmed, Azure AD authentication, scoped firewall rules, SQL Auditing to a storage account); a geo-replicated secondary server under an auto-failover group with a tested — not just configured — failover path; a captured Query Store performance baseline; PowerShell/Azure Automation runbooks for maintenance; DACPAC-based CI/CD for schema changes; and a real incident — a failover drill that exposed a connection-string gap — found, fixed, and now backed by a recurring tested-drill schedule and a failover runbook that explicitly checks every connected application by name. Nothing here is more advanced than the tools taught earlier in this path — the point of this series is showing how Azure SQL, Data Factory, Terraform, PowerShell, and Git/CI fit together on one real job, not introducing new tools.

lessons.title: Meeting Thornridge Insurance: Why a Disk Failure Almost Took Down Claims
lessons.summary: The discovery meeting: how one degraded RAID array finally got a 13-year-old database migration funded, and what you have to learn before touching a single server.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
Over the next 20 videos, you'll walk through one complete, start-to-finish Azure Database Engineer engagement for a fictional regional insurer, **Thornridge Insurance** — roughly 340,000 active auto, home, and umbrella policies, a claims team that processes around 2,400 claims a day, and a core policy-and-claims database, `PolicyClaimsDB`, that has run on the same on-premises SQL Server for over thirteen years. You've been brought in to migrate that database to Azure SQL Database and, more importantly, to build around it everything that aging server never had: real security hardening, high availability and disaster recovery that's actually been tested with a real failover, a real performance baseline, and automated maintenance that doesn't depend on one person remembering to run a script.

By the end of this series you'll have moved `PolicyClaimsDB` into Azure, paired it across regions behind a tested auto-failover group, hardened it against the kind of access an insurance company's regulators actually ask about, and automated the maintenance work that used to live entirely in one DBA's head. This video starts where every real engagement like this starts — not with a migration script, but with the meeting where you find out exactly how close this company came to losing that database for good.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine your family keeps every important paper — birth certificates, the deed to the house, old photos — in one box in the basement, for thirteen years, and nobody's ever once practiced what they'd do if that basement flooded. One night, water actually starts seeping toward the box. It gets pulled out just in time, nothing is ruined, but everyone in the house is suddenly very aware that "just in time" and "too late" were about three inches apart. That's the night your family finally agrees to buy a real fireproof safe and put a copy of everything somewhere else too.

That's exactly what happened to Thornridge Insurance, except the box is a computer that stores every policy and every claim, and the flood was a hard drive failing at 11pm on a Friday. Before you build anything new, your very first job is to sit down with the people who were there that night and find out exactly what almost went wrong — because you can't design something safer until you understand precisely how the old thing almost failed.
lessons.explainProfessional:
This is the discovery meeting, and the detail that matters most in it isn't the headline — "we had a disk failure" — it's the specific failure chain underneath that headline, because that chain tells you exactly which guarantees the current environment was quietly missing. A single failed disk in a RAID array is routine; most arrays are built to absorb exactly that. What makes this story worth telling in a kickoff meeting is how close the second failure came, and how long an actual restore would have taken if backups hadn't been current — both of which are facts you only get by asking specific, uncomfortable questions rather than accepting "we had a scare, now we want to move to the cloud" as the whole story.

You'll hear this story from three different vantage points in this lesson, and each one surfaces a different real requirement. Thornridge's VP of IT, Renata Osei, cares about never having this conversation again — she wants resilience that doesn't depend on luck. Yolanda Pierce, the Director of Claims Operations, cares about something narrower and just as real: her adjusters process claims against this database every business hour, and any downtime is measured in claims that can't be filed, not abstract "system availability." And Carl Dunmore, the on-prem DBA who has personally kept this server alive for thirteen years, knows the uncomfortable truth none of the slides will say out loud: the backups were current because he's disciplined about log backups, not because the environment was ever actually designed to survive this. Your job this lesson is to get all three of those truths on the record before you design anything.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 — Know the failure chain before you walk into the room

Don't show up to a discovery meeting and just ask "what happened?" Come in already able to ask the second and third question, because the first answer is never the whole story:

- Did one disk fail, or did a second disk in the same array start showing warning signs too?
- How old was the most recent successful backup when the failure happened?
- Had a real restore of this database ever actually been tested, end to end, before that night?
- How long would a real restore have taken, and what would the business have done during that window?
- Is this the first scare, or has something like this nearly happened before and gotten quietly patched over?

## Step 2 — Run the meeting and let the details surface on their own

Renata Osei, Thornridge's VP of IT, opens the meeting the way these meetings usually open — with the headline, not the detail:

```
RENATA: Three weeks ago we came about as close as you can come to
        losing our entire claims database without actually losing it.
        That's why this project finally has a budget. I want you to
        hear exactly what happened from Carl, because I don't think
        the board fully understood it either until he walked us
        through it.
```

Carl Dunmore, who has been the sole DBA on this server for thirteen years, fills in the chain:

```
CARL: It's an eight-disk RAID-10 array, local storage, no SAN. One
      disk failed outright around 11pm Friday. That's normally a
      non-event -- RAID-10 is built to survive exactly one disk down.
      What I didn't love was that a second disk, in the same mirrored
      pair, started logging predictive-failure warnings about five
      hours later. If that second disk had actually gone before I
      swapped the first one, that whole array goes down, and we're
      restoring from backup on hardware that's thirteen years old.

YOU:  Walk me through the backups. If that had happened, what were
      you actually restoring from, and how old was it?

CARL: Full backup every night at 11pm, log backups every 15 minutes.
      So worst case, we lose fifteen minutes of claims activity -- not
      nothing, but not catastrophic. The part that actually scared me
      is that I'd never run that exact restore end to end before. When
      I dry-ran it that weekend to make sure we were covered, the
      runbook pointed at a backup path that had been moved two years
      earlier. It still would have worked, but it cost me real hours
      figuring that out under pressure, on a system where every hour
      down is a few hundred claims that can't be touched.

YOLANDA: And that's the part I care about. My adjusters process
         somewhere around 2,400 claims a day in a normal week, and
         closer to 4,000 after a bad hailstorm. An outage on a Monday
         morning isn't an IT problem to me, it's a backlog my team is
         still digging out of two weeks later.
```

## Step 3 — Write the incident summary while the details are still fresh

Turn the conversation into one page, in plain language, before anything gets softened in the retelling:

```
THORNRIDGE INSURANCE — INCIDENT SUMMARY (DISCOVERY INPUT)

What happened:     One disk failed in the production RAID-10 array
                    supporting PolicyClaimsDB. A second disk in the
                    same mirrored pair logged predictive-failure
                    warnings ~5 hours later.
How close:          One more disk failure in that pair would have
                    taken the entire array offline.
Data loss exposure: Up to 15 minutes, based on log backup frequency
                    (none actually occurred).
Untested assumption: A full restore had never been run end to end
                    before this incident; the documented runbook was
                    out of date.
Business impact:    None this time. Avoided impact if it had gone
                    the other way: unknown hours of claims-processing
                    downtime during a period averaging ~2,400 claims/day.
Server age:         ~13 years old, on-premises, single array, no
                    secondary site.
```

## Step 4 — Get the story confirmed in writing before moving to requirements

Send this summary back to Renata, Carl, and Yolanda and ask each of them directly: "Is this an accurate account of what happened and what was at risk?" Getting that agreement now matters later — in the next lesson, every testable requirement you write traces back to a specific line in this incident summary, and later in this engagement, when real high-availability testing happens, this is the document that explains why "configured" was never going to be good enough on its own.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Got the full failure chain from Carl: single disk failure in a RAID-10 array, but a second disk in the same mirrored pair started throwing predictive-failure warnings about five hours later — one more failure away from the whole array going down. Backups were current, so actual data-loss exposure was under 15 minutes, but the restore itself had never been tested end to end, and the documented runbook pointed at a backup path that moved two years ago. That gap — untested recovery, not missing backups — is exactly what the new HA/DR design has to close.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: Documented the incident that triggered this project: a near-miss disk failure on a 13-year-old server, where the backups happened to be current but recovery had never actually been drill-tested. All three stakeholders — IT, Claims Operations, and the DBA who's run this server for over a decade — have confirmed this account in writing, which is what the rest of the requirements and the eventual go-live sign-off will be measured against.
workplaceExplanation.executive: Three weeks ago, Thornridge came within one disk failure of losing its entire claims database, and only avoided real data loss by luck and a disciplined backup schedule — not by design. That's the specific risk this project closes: moving to an environment where resilience is tested and proven, not something we find out about during an actual emergency.

lessons.title: Turning 'Make This Reliable' Into a Testable Migration Requirement
lessons.summary: Converting the incident summary and Renata's 'make this reliable' into specific, measurable RPO/RTO, security, and performance requirements the whole project can be built and judged against.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
The discovery meeting gave you a real incident and three honest accounts of what nearly went wrong — but "make this reliable" and "we need real security" are not requirements yet, they're intentions. This lesson turns them into something you can actually design against: a written Recovery Point Objective and Recovery Time Objective pulled directly out of the incident summary's own numbers, specific security controls tied to what an insurance company's regulators and auditors actually expect, and a measurable performance baseline so "is it fast enough" has an actual answer instead of a feeling.

This is the document every later technical decision in this series answers to. When the migration plan gets built around Data Factory, when the failover group gets configured, when security hardening gets applied to the new Azure SQL server, and when that environment eventually gets tested for real — all of it traces back to a specific, numbered line in the document you write in this lesson, not to a vague memory of what Renata said she wanted.
lessons.explainSimple:
Remember the family with the box in the basement? After the almost-flood, everyone agrees they want things to be "safer." But "safer" doesn't tell the plumber what to actually build. Does safer mean the box survives a flood up to the ceiling? Up to one foot? Does it mean they can get the papers back in five minutes, or is a day okay? Until someone writes those numbers down, two people can both say "yes, that's safer" about two completely different houses.

That's what we're doing in this lesson for Thornridge. "Make this reliable" turns into actual numbers: if something breaks, how much work are we allowed to lose, and how fast do we have to be back up and running? Once those numbers are written down, everyone — you, Renata, Carl, Yolanda — is building toward the exact same target instead of three different guesses at what "reliable" means.
lessons.explainProfessional:
A requirement that can't be falsified isn't a requirement — it's a hope, and hopes are what Thornridge was quietly running on for thirteen years. The two numbers that matter most for any database migration like this are Recovery Point Objective — how much data can we afford to lose if something fails — and Recovery Time Objective — how long can the business tolerate being down. Both of these should be pulled directly from what you already learned in discovery, not invented in a vacuum: the incident summary already told you that a 15-minute log backup interval kept actual exposure under 15 minutes, which gives you a real, defensible starting RPO target, and Yolanda's claims-volume numbers give you a concrete way to express what an hour of downtime actually costs in claims that can't be filed.

Security requirements need the same specificity. "Make it secure" resolves into concrete controls: encryption at rest and in transit (table stakes, but worth stating explicitly for an audit trail), Azure AD-based authentication instead of legacy SQL logins wherever possible, least-privilege access so Carl's thirteen years of accumulated sysadmin-level access on the old box doesn't get copied forward unexamined, and auditing that can answer "who accessed this policyholder's data and when" — a question an insurance regulator can and will ask. Performance requirements need a baseline before they need a target: you can't promise the new environment is faster until you've measured what the old one actually does today, on real queries, under real load — which is exactly what makes the performance-baseline work in a later lesson possible.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 — Pull every testable number out of what you already know

Go back through the Lesson 1 incident summary and Yolanda's numbers and extract what's already measurable, instead of inventing new targets from nothing:

```
FROM DISCOVERY:
  - Log backups every 15 minutes -> real data-loss exposure was <15 min
  - Claims volume: ~2,400/day normal, ~4,000/day after a weather event
  - A full restore had never been tested end to end
  - Server is ~13 years old with no secondary site at all
```

## Step 2 — Draft RPO and RTO as numbers, and defend each one

```
RECOVERY POINT OBJECTIVE (RPO): 5 minutes or less.
  Why: the old environment's own backup cadence already proved 15
  minutes of exposure was tolerable in a true worst case. Azure SQL's
  native backup and geo-replication can comfortably beat that, so the
  target should reflect what the new platform can actually guarantee,
  not just match the old bar.

RECOVERY TIME OBJECTIVE (RTO): under 15 minutes for a regional outage,
  achieved via a tested auto-failover group -- not a multi-hour manual
  restore like the one Carl described dry-running.
  Why: at ~2,400 claims/day, every hour of claims-system downtime
  during business hours is roughly 300 claims that can't be filed or
  updated. A target measured in minutes, not hours, is what actually
  changes the business's exposure.
```

## Step 3 — Turn "make it secure" into named, checkable controls

```
SECURITY REQUIREMENTS:
  SEC-1: All data encrypted at rest and in transit by default
         (verification: confirm TDE and enforced TLS on the new server).
  SEC-2: Azure AD authentication required for all human administrative
         access; legacy SQL logins limited to service accounts only
         (verification: review the server's configured authentication
         mode and login list).
  SEC-3: Access reviewed and reduced to least privilege -- Carl's
         current sysadmin-level access on the old box gets re-scoped,
         not copied forward as-is (verification: documented access
         review, signed off by Renata).
  SEC-4: Auditing enabled that can answer "who accessed which
         policyholder's records, and when" for at least 90 days
         (verification: test query against audit logs for a sample
         policy number).
```

## Step 4 — Turn "is it fast enough" into a baseline-first requirement

```
PERFORMANCE REQUIREMENT:
  PERF-1: Before any migration work begins, capture real baseline
          numbers from the current on-prem server -- the slowest
          claims-lookup queries Yolanda's team actually runs, and how
          long they currently take.
          Why first: without this number, nobody can later prove the
          new environment performs as well as or better than what it
          replaced -- "it feels fast" isn't a verification method.
```

## Step 5 — Review it line by line with Renata, Carl, and Yolanda

Read each requirement out loud and ask for a direct yes or no, the same way you'd confirm the incident summary. Carl in particular needs to hear SEC-3 said plainly — re-scoping his own long-standing access is a real change, and it goes much better coming from a documented requirement everyone agreed to than as a surprise during implementation.

## Step 6 — Version and date the requirements document

Save it as something like `Thornridge_V1_Migration_Requirements_v1.md`. This is the document Lesson 3 uses to draw the scope line, and the document that later HA/DR testing in this series gets measured against.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Converted 'make this reliable' into numbers: RPO of 5 minutes or less, RTO under 15 minutes via a tested failover, not a manual restore. Security requirements are named and checkable — AAD-based auth, least-privilege access review on Carl's own long-standing permissions, encryption at rest and in transit, auditable access logs. Added a baseline-first performance requirement so we have real pre-migration numbers to measure against, not a feeling.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: We now have a signed-off requirements document with actual numbers behind 'reliable' and 'secure' instead of adjectives — specific recovery targets, specific security controls, and a commitment to baseline performance before we touch anything. This is what the migration plan, the security hardening, and the eventual go-live testing all get measured against.
workplaceExplanation.executive: We've turned 'make this reliable' into specific commitments: if something fails, we lose minutes of data, not hours, and we're back up in minutes, not the better part of a day like we nearly were three weeks ago. Security access is being reviewed and tightened as part of this, not just copied over from the old system.

lessons.title: Scoping V1: Migrate and Secure Now, Automate Maintenance Next
lessons.summary: Drawing a hard line around what phase one actually delivers — migration, security hardening, and tested HA/DR — and logging automation and CI/CD as the next phase, not a forgotten promise.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
You now have real, numbered requirements. Before any Azure resource gets provisioned, this lesson draws a hard written line around what V1 of this engagement actually covers, and — just as importantly — writes down what's being deliberately pushed to the next phase instead of quietly dropped. For Thornridge, that line falls in a specific place: V1 gets `PolicyClaimsDB` migrated, secured, and genuinely resilient — a tested failover between two Azure SQL logical servers, not just a configuration that's never been proven. V1 also includes the automation that keeps this environment healthy without anyone's manual intervention — scheduled PowerShell runbooks for maintenance, and a real CI/CD pipeline for schema changes — because a migrated database that's still maintained by hand is the same risk that led to the disk failure, just running in a new location. What's genuinely out of scope for now is anything beyond keeping this one database healthy and deployable: deeper query-level tuning past the initial baseline, and decommissioning the old on-premises hardware, both of which depend on this environment proving itself first.

This is also the document you'll point back to later in this engagement, when the hard part of V1 — actually running a real failover drill instead of trusting that the configuration alone is enough — meets the kind of schedule pressure that tempts a team to call something "tested" because it was configured correctly and nothing has gone wrong yet.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine you're moving your family to a new house because the old one had a scary close call with a flooded basement. On moving day, your little brother starts asking if the new house can also get a trampoline, a treehouse, and a dog. Those might all be great ideas! But if you try to do all of it on moving day, the actual move — getting everyone safely into a sturdier house — takes twice as long and might not happen cleanly at all.

So you write two lists: "this is what we're doing on moving day" (get everyone moved in safely, make sure the new house doesn't have the same flooding problem) and "this is the list for after we're settled" (trampoline, treehouse, dog). Nobody's idea gets thrown away — it's just not happening today, because today has one job.
lessons.explainProfessional:
Scope discipline matters more on a migration-and-security engagement than almost anywhere else, because the two things most tempting to bundle in — "let's also automate everything while we're in there" and "let's also build the CI/CD pipeline now" — are both genuinely good ideas that would each, on their own, extend the timeline for the thing that actually has to ship first: getting Thornridge off a thirteen-year-old single point of failure. The discipline here is the same one from the requirements lesson — every idea that comes up gets an explicit, written disposition, not a shrug — but the stakes are higher, because the item being deferred (automation) is real, it's part of this same client relationship, and it's genuinely coming in the next phase of this exact engagement, not a permanently rejected wish.

The harder scope conversation in this lesson is around HA/DR testing specifically, because it's the item most likely to get quietly shortchanged under schedule pressure. "The failover group is configured" and "the failover group has been proven, with a real failover drill, to actually redirect the application correctly" are two different claims, and only the second one satisfies the RTO requirement from Lesson 2. Writing "a real, executed failover drill, not just a validated configuration" into the V1 definition of done now is what gives you standing later to insist on it even if a go-live date is approaching and everything looks fine on paper.

lessons.title: Choosing the Stack: Azure SQL Database, Not Just a Bigger On-Prem Server
lessons.summary: The first real architecture decision: why Azure SQL Database, not Managed Instance or SQL Server on an Azure VM, fits Thornridge's actual constraints — and the resource names this series uses from here forward.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
With scope locked, this is the first real architecture decision: which Azure SQL deployment option actually hosts `PolicyClaimsDB` going forward. Azure gives you three real choices here — Azure SQL Database (a fully managed, single-database PaaS offering), Azure SQL Managed Instance (near-complete SQL Server surface area, still PaaS), and SQL Server running on an Azure VM (full control, but you're still the one patching and backing it up). This lesson walks through why Azure SQL Database is the right fit for this specific workload, this team, and this requirement set — not because it's the most powerful option, but because it's the one that actually closes the gaps the Lesson 1 incident exposed.

This lesson also fixes the naming this whole engagement uses from here forward: the resource group `rg-thornridge-sql-prod`, the primary logical server `thornridge-sql-server` hosting `PolicyClaimsDB`, and — previewed here, built out fully in a later lesson — a secondary logical server, `thornridge-sql-server-secondary`, paired through an auto-failover group, `thornridge-sql-failover-group`. Every later lesson in this series refers back to these exact names.
lessons.explainSimple:
Think about moving out of an old, unreliable house. You have a few real options: buy a fancier house where someone else still handles all the repairs and the roof (that's like Azure SQL Database), buy a house where you get a bit more control over how rooms are arranged but a maintenance company still handles the big stuff (that's like Managed Instance), or buy a plot of land and build the exact same kind of house yourself, where you're back to fixing your own roof and worrying about your own backups (that's like running SQL Server on your own virtual machine).

For one family moving out of one aging house, the first option usually makes the most sense — you get real safety without taking on a second full-time job as your own maintenance crew. That's exactly the trade-off Thornridge is making: picking the option where Microsoft handles patching, backups, and the physical reliability of the hardware, so Carl's team can focus on the data itself instead of babysitting a server rack.
lessons.explainProfessional:
The decision here comes down to matching the deployment model to what actually broke, not to raw capability. SQL Server on an Azure VM gives you the most control — full OS access, every SQL Server feature, cross-database queries, SQL Server Agent exactly as Carl already knows it — but it also hands you back the exact two responsibilities that caused the Lesson 1 incident in the first place: you are still patching the OS, still managing the storage array underneath the database, and still responsible for testing your own backup and restore process, just on someone else's hardware. For a small IT shop that just spent three weeks finding out its restore runbook was stale, that's not the win it sounds like.

Azure SQL Managed Instance narrows that gap — it's PaaS, Microsoft handles patching and the underlying infrastructure — and it's a genuinely strong fit for workloads that lean on cross-database queries, SQL Server Agent jobs, or Linked Servers. `PolicyClaimsDB` is a single, self-contained database with no meaningful cross-database dependencies, so Managed Instance's biggest advantages don't actually apply here, while its higher baseline cost and longer provisioning time would. Azure SQL Database is the option that matches Thornridge's actual shape: a single production database, a small team that doesn't want a second infrastructure to operate, and — critically for the HA/DR requirement locked in Lesson 3 — native support for Active Geo-Replication and auto-failover groups without having to build or script that resilience by hand. The RPO/RTO targets from Lesson 2 are something Azure SQL Database gives you largely out of the box; on a VM, you'd be rebuilding a weaker version of the same thing yourself, which is precisely the kind of unproven, hand-built resilience this whole engagement exists to replace. (This same stack is also building toward the DP-300 certification, though the exam's exact scope and format should always be checked against Microsoft's current, official requirements rather than assumed from a course.)

lessons.title: Planning the Migration Path With Data Factory
lessons.summary: Mapping the one-time bulk copy, the incremental sync that keeps both databases in agreement during cutover, and a written cutover-and-rollback sequence -- before a single pipeline is built.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
With Azure SQL Database chosen as the target in the last lesson, this lesson plans exactly how ten-plus years of `PolicyClaimsDB` data gets from Thornridge's on-prem SQL Server into Azure without a multi-day outage and without repeating the near-miss that started this whole project. The answer has two parts, both carried by one Azure Data Factory pipeline, `pl_migrate_policyclaims`: a one-time **bulk copy** of everything that exists today, and an **incremental sync** that keeps the on-prem and Azure copies agreeing with each other during the window between "the bulk copy finished" and "the claims app is actually pointed at Azure."

Nothing gets built in this lesson -- no pipeline, no linked service. This is the plan the next implementation lessons build against, including the exact sequence of steps for the cutover itself and what happens if something goes wrong partway through it.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine moving a filing cabinet full of insurance paperwork into a new office, but the old office has to keep handling new paperwork every day until moving day actually arrives. You wouldn't just carry the whole cabinet over once and call it done -- new folders would keep showing up at the old office after you left. So you move everything once, then every so often you carry over just the *new* folders that showed up since the last trip, until moving day, when you do one final small trip, lock the old office's front door, and tell everyone to use the new address from now on.

That's the plan here: one big copy of everything, then small top-up copies to catch anything new, then one final switch.
lessons.explainProfessional:
This is a classic minimal-downtime migration pattern, and the two mechanisms need to be planned as genuinely separate problems. The bulk copy is a throughput problem: move ~10 years of `PolicyClaimsDB` data once, as fast and as safely as possible, using an ADF Copy Activity reading from the on-prem SQL Server through a Self-Hosted Integration Runtime (SHIR) -- required because Azure Data Factory's managed, cloud-hosted IR has no network path to a server sitting inside Thornridge's own data center.

The incremental sync is a correctness problem: once the bulk copy finishes, the on-prem database keeps taking live writes from the claims app, so Azure immediately starts drifting out of date. We close that gap with a per-table watermark column (`ModifiedDateUtc` where it exists reliably) tracked in a control table, plus SQL Server Change Tracking specifically on the `Policies` table, which doesn't have a trustworthy modified-date column to watermark against. Both mechanisms feed the same incremental copy pattern in ADF: look up the last-synced watermark, copy only rows newer than it, upsert rather than blind-insert so a re-run is never destructive. The cutover itself is the part most migrations get wrong by treating it as a live judgment call instead of a rehearsed sequence -- we're writing that sequence, and its rollback, down now, before anyone is standing in front of a terminal at 11pm.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Separate the two problems on paper first

```
BULK COPY        -- move everything that exists today, once
INCREMENTAL SYNC -- keep on-prem and Azure agreeing, every N minutes,
                    from "bulk copy done" until "cutover complete"
CUTOVER          -- the exact sequence that ends with the app writing
                    to Azure and on-prem no longer the system of record
```

Both the bulk copy and the incremental sync run inside the same ADF pipeline, `pl_migrate_policyclaims`, as separate activities -- one full-load path, one incremental path, selected by a pipeline parameter.

## Step 2 -- Plan the bulk copy: Self-Hosted IR + Copy Activity

The on-prem SQL Server has no public endpoint, so a lightweight Self-Hosted Integration Runtime gets installed on a VM inside Thornridge's network with a line of sight to both the on-prem server and the internet:

```json
{
  "name": "ls_onprem_sqlserver",
  "type": "Microsoft.DataFactory/factories/linkedservices",
  "properties": {
    "type": "SqlServer",
    "connectVia": { "referenceName": "shir-thornridge-onprem", "type": "IntegrationRuntimeReference" },
    "typeProperties": { "connectionString": "Server=THORN-SQL01;Database=PolicyClaimsDB;Trusted_Connection=True;" }
  }
}
```

Each source table gets its own Copy Activity inside `pl_migrate_policyclaims`, sink set to the matching table in Azure SQL `PolicyClaimsDB`, batched with staged copy enabled (via Blob storage) since that's materially faster for a database this size than a direct network path alone.

## Step 3 -- Plan the incremental sync: watermark table + Change Tracking

```sql
-- control table, created in a small ops schema on the Azure side
CREATE TABLE ops.sync_watermark (
    table_name     SYSNAME NOT NULL PRIMARY KEY,
    last_watermark DATETIME2 NOT NULL,
    updated_at     DATETIME2 NOT NULL DEFAULT SYSUTCDATETIME()
);
```

For tables with a trustworthy `ModifiedDateUtc` column (`Claims`, `Payments`, `Endorsements`), the incremental Copy Activity's source query is parameterized against `ops.sync_watermark`:

```sql
SELECT * FROM dbo.Claims
WHERE ModifiedDateUtc > @last_watermark
  AND ModifiedDateUtc <= @sync_run_time;
```

`Policies` has no reliable modified-date column, so we enable SQL Server Change Tracking on it instead, and the incremental activity reads `CHANGETABLE(CHANGES dbo.Policies, @last_sync_version)` -- this catches updates and deletes a watermark column alone would miss. Every incremental run upserts (`MERGE`, not `INSERT`) into the Azure side, so re-running a sync after a failure never double-applies a change.

## Step 4 -- Write the cutover sequence down, in order

```
1. Run final bulk copy validation: row counts + checksum on key columns
   reconcile between on-prem and Azure for every table.
2. Freeze on-prem writes: put the claims app into read-only maintenance
   mode for a planned 15-minute window.
3. Run one final incremental sync pass to catch anything written in
   the seconds before the freeze.
4. Re-validate row counts match exactly.
5. Point the claims app's connection string at Azure SQL and lift
   maintenance mode.
6. Monitor the app against Azure for a defined soak period before
   decommissioning anything on-prem.
```

## Step 5 -- Write the rollback plan before you need it

If step 4's validation fails, the on-prem server stays the system of record -- maintenance mode lifts, the app keeps writing on-prem, and the incremental sync keeps running to narrow the gap before trying again. The on-prem server stays live and untouched for a minimum soak period after cutover specifically so this rollback path is never theoretical.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Locked the migration mechanics: `pl_migrate_policyclaims` runs the bulk copy through a Self-Hosted IR since the on-prem box has no public endpoint, then switches to incremental mode using a watermark control table for most tables and Change Tracking specifically on Policies, which doesn't have a usable modified-date column. The cutover sequence and rollback trigger are both written down now, before any of this touches production.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: We've mapped exactly how the historical data moves over, how we keep the two databases in sync during the transition window, and the precise step-by-step cutover sequence -- including what we do if validation fails partway through. That sequence is what we'll walk through with the team before the actual cutover date is set.
workplaceExplanation.executive: We've planned the move so the claims system keeps working normally right up until the switch, with a tested rollback path if anything doesn't check out on cutover day. Nothing about this plan risks a repeat of the outage scare that started this project.

lessons.title: Planning Security: Encryption, Authentication, and Auditing
lessons.summary: Confirming encryption-at-rest is actually on, replacing SQL logins with Azure AD authentication, locking down network access, and routing a full audit trail to a storage account -- before the server exists.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding: `PolicyClaimsDB` holds policyholder names, addresses, claim details, and payment information for a regional insurer -- exactly the kind of data a security plan has to get right the first time, not patch in afterward. This lesson plans the four security decisions that have to be settled before Lesson 8 provisions a single real resource: confirming Transparent Data Encryption is genuinely protecting the database rather than just assumed to be, replacing SQL logins with Azure AD authentication everywhere that's realistic, deciding how the server is reachable on the network at all, and making sure every login and every write to a claims table lands in an audit trail nobody can quietly turn off.
lessons.explainSimple:
Think about a bank vault. You wouldn't just trust that the walls are thick -- you'd actually check. You wouldn't hand out a key to anyone who asks -- you'd check ID against a list first. You wouldn't leave the vault door reachable from the street -- you'd put it behind other locked doors too. And you'd keep a logbook of exactly who opened the vault and when, so if something ever goes missing, you know who was there.

That's what we're planning for Thornridge's new database: checking the encryption is really on, checking identities properly instead of handing out simple passwords, limiting who can even reach the front door, and keeping a logbook of everything that happens inside.
lessons.explainProfessional:
Azure SQL Database enables Transparent Data Encryption by default on every new database, encrypting data and log files at rest with a platform-managed key -- but "on by default" is a fact to verify, not assume, since it can be explicitly disabled by a prior administrator or a misconfigured deployment template, and an insurer's compliance posture needs proof, not a default. Authentication is the second pillar: SQL logins are username/password pairs that live inside the database and have no connection to Thornridge's existing identity provider, which means no centralized password policy, no MFA, and no ability to revoke access the moment someone leaves the company. Azure AD authentication fixes all four by letting the database trust identities Thornridge's IT team already manages centrally -- so wherever a human or a service genuinely needs database access, that access is an Azure AD identity, not a standalone SQL login.

Network reachability and auditing are the two pillars people plan last and regret planning last. A database's firewall should default to denying everything and explicitly allow only what's known -- the Self-Hosted IR's outbound IP during migration, and Thornridge's corporate IP ranges afterward -- with a private endpoint over a VNet noted as the real end-state once Thornridge's network team has VNet connectivity ready, not something to delay the whole project waiting on. SQL Auditing writes every login attempt and every data-modification statement to a storage account outside the database itself, specifically so the audit trail survives even a compromised or deleted database -- for an insurer, that's not a nice-to-have, it's the record a regulator or an internal investigation will eventually ask to see.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Plan to verify TDE, not just assume it

Azure SQL turns TDE on by default for every new database, but the plan is to check this explicitly the moment `PolicyClaimsDB` exists, not trust the default silently -- a prior administrator, a misconfigured deployment template, or a well-meaning troubleshooting step can all disable it, and "the portal probably has it on" is not something an insurer can put in a compliance questionnaire:

```sql
SELECT db.name, dek.encryption_state, dek.encryptor_type
FROM sys.dm_database_encryption_keys dek
JOIN sys.databases db ON db.database_id = dek.database_id
WHERE db.name = 'PolicyClaimsDB';
-- encryption_state = 3 means encrypted; anything else gets escalated
-- before the database is considered ready for real data.
```

v1 uses the service-managed key (Microsoft-managed, rotated automatically). A customer-managed key held in Azure Key Vault is logged as a v2 candidate once Thornridge's compliance team finishes its key-custody policy -- noted now, in writing, not silently dropped because it wasn't ready in time for provisioning.

## Step 2 -- Plan the Azure AD authentication model

```sql
-- Azure AD admin set on the logical server (via Terraform in Lesson 8)
-- Human + service access created as contained users, not SQL logins:
CREATE USER [svc-adf-policyclaims] FROM EXTERNAL PROVIDER;
ALTER ROLE db_datareader ADD MEMBER [svc-adf-policyclaims];
ALTER ROLE db_datawriter ADD MEMBER [svc-adf-policyclaims];

CREATE USER [DBA-OnCall-Group] FROM EXTERNAL PROVIDER;
```

`svc-adf-policyclaims` is the identity `pl_migrate_policyclaims` (Lesson 5) authenticates as, via a managed identity -- no connection string password stored anywhere. One SQL login is planned as a deliberate, time-boxed exception: the legacy claims app's existing connection code expects SQL authentication, and that gets retired in a follow-up lesson once the app itself is updated, not left in place indefinitely.

## Step 3 -- Plan network access: locked firewall now, private endpoint later

```
v1 (at provisioning):
  - Deny all by default ("Allow Azure services" left OFF)
  - Explicit firewall rule for the Self-Hosted IR VM's static outbound IP
  - Explicit firewall rule for Thornridge's corporate office IP range
v2 (logged, not v1 scope):
  - Private Endpoint over a VNet, once Thornridge's network team has
    VNet peering ready between the office network and Azure
```

## Step 4 -- Plan SQL Auditing to a storage account

Auditing has to write somewhere the database itself can't quietly erase, which rules out logging to a table inside `PolicyClaimsDB` -- if the database is ever the thing under investigation, its own internal log is exactly the evidence that can't be trusted. A dedicated storage account, outside the database's blast radius entirely, is the plan:

```bash
az sql db audit-policy update \
  --resource-group rg-thornridge-sql-prod \
  --server thornridge-sql-server \
  --name PolicyClaimsDB \
  --state Enabled \
  --storage-account thornridgesqlauditlogs \
  --retention-days 365
```

Action groups in scope: `FAILED_DATABASE_AUTHENTICATION_GROUP` and `SUCCESSFUL_DATABASE_AUTHENTICATION_GROUP` (every login attempt, successful or not), plus data-modification activity scoped specifically to the `Claims`, `Policies`, and `Payments` tables rather than every table in the database -- broad enough to answer "who touched this claim and when," narrow enough that the audit log itself doesn't become an unmanageable firehose. Retention is set to 365 days to match Thornridge's existing records-retention policy for claims data, and the storage account itself gets its own restrictive access policy, since an audit trail anyone can edit isn't really an audit trail.

## Step 5 -- Plan a review cadence, not just a collection pipeline

An audit log nobody ever reads is just storage cost. The plan includes a monthly review of failed-authentication spikes and a standing rule: any access to `Claims` or `Payments` outside the service identities and the DBA group listed in Step 2 gets flagged automatically, not discovered three months later during an unrelated investigation.

## Step 6 -- Write the one-paragraph security posture down

```
"Every identity touching PolicyClaimsDB is an Azure AD identity unless
explicitly logged as a time-boxed exception. Encryption at rest is
verified, not assumed. Network access defaults to denied. Every login
and every write to a sensitive table is recorded somewhere the
database itself cannot erase."
```

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Locked the security plan: TDE gets verified via `sys.dm_database_encryption_keys` the moment the database exists, not assumed from the default. Azure AD authentication replaces SQL logins everywhere except one time-boxed exception for the legacy app, with ADF connecting through a managed identity, not a stored password. Firewall defaults to deny-all with explicit rules for the SHIR VM and our office range; private endpoint is logged for v2 once networking has VNet peering ready. Auditing writes logins and claims-table writes to a storage account with a year of retention.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: We've planned exactly how access to the new database is controlled and recorded before it exists -- centralized identity instead of shared passwords, a locked-down network boundary, and a full audit trail that lives outside the database itself. One temporary exception for the legacy app is documented with a planned retirement date, not left open-ended.
workplaceExplanation.executive: We're planning this database the way an insurer's data needs to be handled from day one -- encryption confirmed, access tied to the identities IT already manages and can revoke immediately, the network locked down to only what needs it, and a complete record of who touched what. That's the kind of posture a regulator or an auditor expects to see already in place, not retrofitted after something goes wrong.

lessons.title: Planning High Availability and Disaster Recovery
lessons.summary: Separating Azure SQL's automatic, included local HA from the explicit, cross-region failover group it still needs -- and planning to prove the whole thing with a real failover drill once it's built.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding: This lesson plans the two layers of resilience `PolicyClaimsDB` needs, and -- just as important -- makes sure nobody on the project confuses them. Azure SQL Database already includes automatic local high availability inside whichever region it runs in; that part requires no extra setup. What it does not include automatically is protection against losing an entire Azure region, which is exactly the kind of event a regional insurer's claims system cannot be offline for. That protection -- Active Geo-Replication under an auto-failover group, with a secondary logical server in a different region -- has to be explicitly planned and built. This lesson draws that line clearly, and commits the project to proving the result actually works with a real failover drill once it exists, rather than trusting it untested.
lessons.explainSimple:
Think about a house with a backup generator built into the wall versus a second house in another city. The built-in generator kicks on automatically the moment the power flickers -- you don't have to do anything, and it's already there. But if a hurricane takes out the whole town, the generator doesn't help; you need an actual second house somewhere else, with your important things already copied over, and a plan for how everyone gets there and moves back in.

Azure SQL gives Thornridge the built-in generator automatically. The second house in another city -- the part that protects against something big enough to take out an entire region -- is something we have to deliberately build and plan for, including practicing the move before it's ever needed for real.
lessons.explainProfessional:
The distinction worth getting exactly right here is automatic-and-included versus explicit-and-built. Azure SQL Database's built-in high availability runs underneath every database regardless of tier -- in the General Purpose tier it relies on remote, replicated storage with a standby compute node; in Business Critical it adds local SSD storage and up to three synchronously replicated secondary replicas via the same technology that underlies Always On Availability Groups. Either way, this protects against a node failure or, with zone redundancy enabled, an availability-zone failure inside one region -- and it requires zero additional architecture from us. For a mid-size insurer's workload with real but not extreme read-latency demands, General Purpose with zone redundancy enabled is the right balance for `PolicyClaimsDB`; Business Critical is logged as a future upsize if read-heavy reporting workloads ever need an offloadable readable secondary.

What that tier choice does not cover is an entire Azure region becoming unavailable -- a rare but real event, and the one category of failure this project explicitly exists to never be caught flat-footed by again. That requires Active Geo-Replication, set up as an auto-failover group (`thornridge-sql-failover-group`) pairing the primary logical server (`thornridge-sql-server`) with a secondary logical server (`thornridge-sql-server-secondary`) provisioned in a different Azure region. The detail that matters most operationally: applications must connect through the failover group's listener endpoint, not the primary server's own hostname directly -- the listener is what silently redirects connections to whichever server is currently primary after a failover, while a direct connection string to the primary server's hostname has no idea a failover even happened. We're writing that requirement down here, in planning, specifically because it's the kind of detail that's trivial to get right during setup and easy to quietly get wrong under deadline pressure. And because an HA/DR setup that has never actually failed over is a plan, not a proven capability, this lesson commits the project to a real, scheduled failover drill once the failover group exists -- verifying actual RTO against the target below, not just that the Azure portal shows both servers healthy.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Name the two layers of resilience separately

```
LAYER 1 -- Built-in local HA
  Scope:     protects against a node or availability-zone failure
             WITHIN one Azure region
  Setup:     automatic, included in every Azure SQL database tier,
             zone redundancy is a checkbox, not a build
  Covers:    hardware failure, a single zone going down
  Does NOT cover: the whole region becoming unavailable

LAYER 2 -- Active Geo-Replication / auto-failover group
  Scope:     protects against losing an entire Azure region
  Setup:     explicit -- a second logical server in a different
             region, paired under a named failover group
  Covers:    regional outage
  Requires:  applications connect via the failover group LISTENER,
             never the primary server's hostname directly
```

## Step 2 -- Choose the service tier and local HA configuration

```
DECISION: General Purpose tier, zone redundancy ENABLED
WHY:      Business Critical's extra local replicas and lower latency
          aren't justified by PolicyClaimsDB's current read/write
          profile; zone redundancy on General Purpose already covers
          the realistic local-failure scenarios at a sustainable cost.
LOGGED:   Business Critical noted as a future upsize if a read-heavy
          analytics/reporting workload later needs an offloadable
          readable secondary.
```

This decision gets written down with its reasoning attached, not just its conclusion, because it's exactly the kind of choice that gets second-guessed later by someone who only sees "General Purpose" on an invoice and assumes it was the cheap option rather than the deliberately right-sized one.

## Step 3 -- Plan the auto-failover group

```bash
az sql server create \
  --name thornridge-sql-server-secondary \
  --resource-group rg-thornridge-sql-prod \
  --location centralus   # primary runs in eastus2

az sql failover-group create \
  --name thornridge-sql-failover-group \
  --resource-group rg-thornridge-sql-prod \
  --server thornridge-sql-server \
  --partner-server thornridge-sql-server-secondary \
  --add-db PolicyClaimsDB \
  --failover-policy Automatic \
  --grace-period 1
```

The app's connection string target is planned as `thornridge-sql-failover-group.database.windows.net` -- the listener -- never `thornridge-sql-server.database.windows.net` directly. That single detail is written here as a hard requirement specifically because it's the kind of thing that's easy to get right in a planning document and easy to get wrong in a rushed app config.

## Step 4 -- Set explicit RTO/RPO targets

```
LOCAL HA (Layer 1):     RTO: seconds to ~30s     RPO: 0 (synchronous)
REGIONAL DR (Layer 2):  RTO: target < 1 hour      RPO: < 5 seconds
                        (automatic failover policy, 1-hour grace period
                        before Azure triggers it unassisted)
```

## Step 5 -- Commit to a real failover drill, in writing, before this is trusted

```
"Once the failover group exists, we will run a planned, scheduled
failover drill against it -- not a tabletop exercise -- and measure
actual time-to-reconnect for the claims app against the RTO target
above. An HA/DR configuration that has never been tested is a
hypothesis, not a capability."
```

The drill plan itself gets three concrete commitments now, before anyone is tempted to skip them later under deadline pressure: it runs against a real, scheduled maintenance window rather than "whenever there's time," someone is explicitly assigned to watch the claims app reconnect and time it rather than just confirming the Azure portal shows the failover completed, and the result -- pass or fail -- gets written down and reviewed by the team, not just the person who ran it.

## Step 6 -- Note what the drill is specifically guarding against

A failover group's configuration on the database side can be entirely correct and the overall system can still fail over badly, because a database setting alone can't verify everything the application layer is doing. The drill has to confirm the whole chain end-to-end -- including how the claims app itself actually behaves the moment the primary changes -- not just that Azure's own health indicators look correct in the portal. That's the gap a real drill is designed to surface, which is exactly why this lesson commits to running one rather than treating the failover group's existence as proof enough on its own.

This commitment is the thread that carries forward into the series' later troubleshooting lessons.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Separated the HA plan into two layers so nobody confuses them: built-in zone-redundant HA on General Purpose covers node/zone failure automatically, no setup needed. Regional DR is the explicit piece -- an auto-failover group pairing `thornridge-sql-server` with a secondary in a different region, with the app required to connect through the failover group listener, never the primary server's hostname directly. RTO/RPO targets are set, and we're committing now to a real failover drill once this is built, not just trusting the portal's green checkmarks.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: We've planned two separate layers of protection: one that's automatic and included with the database tier, and one -- cross-region disaster recovery -- that we have to explicitly build and, importantly, actually test with a real drill before we consider it proven. That drill is already on the plan, not an afterthought.
workplaceExplanation.executive: Your claims database will be protected against both a local hardware failure, which is handled automatically, and a much bigger event like losing an entire Azure region, which we're building explicit protection for. And we're not just going to assume that protection works -- we're planning to actually test it with a real failover before we call it done.

lessons.title: Provisioning Azure SQL With Terraform
lessons.summary: Opening Terraform for the first time to provision the real resource group, logical server, and PolicyClaimsDB -- turning three lessons of planning into actual infrastructure.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
Planning is done -- this is the first lesson where real infrastructure gets created. We're writing the Terraform configuration that stands up `rg-thornridge-sql-prod`, the primary logical server `thornridge-sql-server` with the Azure AD-only authentication model planned in Lesson 6, the `PolicyClaimsDB` database with the zone-redundant General Purpose tier decided in Lesson 7, and the locked-down firewall rules that allow in exactly the Self-Hosted IR host and Thornridge's corporate IP range -- nothing else, by default.

This lesson doesn't yet provision the secondary server or the failover group from Lesson 7, or run the migration pipeline from Lesson 5 -- those are later lessons. What matters here is that every name and every setting in this configuration is a direct, traceable answer to a decision made in the last three videos, not a new one invented on the spot inside a `.tf` file.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine you've already decided exactly what your new house needs -- how many rooms, what the locks look like, which doors are allowed to open from the street. Terraform is like a very detailed, very obedient contractor: you hand it a written blueprint, and it builds exactly what the blueprint says, in the right order, every time, instead of you manually laying each brick by hand and hoping you remember every detail the same way twice.

In this lesson, we hand that blueprint -- the resource group, the server, the database, the locked front door -- to Terraform for the very first time, and watch it build the real thing in Azure.
lessons.explainProfessional:
Infrastructure as Code earns its keep the moment a resource needs to exist identically in more than one place or needs to be rebuilt exactly after a mistake -- both of which are true here, since this same configuration shape stands up the secondary server in a later lesson, and because manually clicking through the Azure portal leaves no reviewable record of exactly what was configured. The `azurerm` provider's `azurerm_mssql_server` resource is where the Lesson 6 authentication decision becomes real: `azuread_administrator` is set so the server has an Azure AD admin from the moment it exists, and we deliberately don't set a SQL admin login/password pair at all, since the plan was Azure AD authentication as the default, not an exception.

`azurerm_mssql_database`'s `sku_name` of `GP_Gen5_4` plus `zone_redundant = true` is the direct Terraform expression of the Lesson 7 tier decision -- General Purpose, zone-redundant, no Business Critical upsize yet. `azurerm_mssql_firewall_rule` resources are deliberately narrow and explicit, one rule per known IP range, rather than a single permissive range or `0.0.0.0`-style shortcuts, because the Lesson 6 plan was deny-by-default. Running `terraform plan` before `apply` here isn't a formality -- it's the last chance to catch a typo in a CIDR range or an accidentally-permissive rule before it's live on a database that's about to hold real policyholder data.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Set up the provider and project structure

```hcl
terraform {
  required_providers {
    azurerm = {
      source  = "hashicorp/azurerm"
      version = "~> 3.90"
    }
  }
}

provider "azurerm" {
  features {}
}
```

## Step 2 -- The resource group

```hcl
resource "azurerm_resource_group" "thornridge_sql_prod" {
  name     = "rg-thornridge-sql-prod"
  location = "eastus2"

  tags = {
    project = "policyclaims-migration"
    owner   = "thornridge-data-platform"
  }
}
```

## Step 3 -- The primary logical server, Azure AD-only (per Lesson 6)

```hcl
resource "azurerm_mssql_server" "primary" {
  name                = "thornridge-sql-server"
  resource_group_name = azurerm_resource_group.thornridge_sql_prod.name
  location            = azurerm_resource_group.thornridge_sql_prod.location
  version             = "12.0"

  # No administrator_login / administrator_login_password --
  # Azure AD authentication is the model, not a SQL admin exception.
  azuread_administrator {
    login_username = "sql-dba-admins"
    object_id      = var.aad_dba_group_object_id
  }

  minimum_tls_version          = "1.2"
  public_network_access_enabled = true  # firewall-restricted, see Step 5
}
```

## Step 4 -- PolicyClaimsDB, zone-redundant General Purpose (per Lesson 7)

```hcl
resource "azurerm_mssql_database" "policyclaims" {
  name           = "PolicyClaimsDB"
  server_id      = azurerm_mssql_server.primary.id
  sku_name       = "GP_Gen5_4"
  zone_redundant = true
  max_size_gb    = 250

  tags = {
    project = "policyclaims-migration"
  }
}
```

## Step 5 -- Firewall rules, locked to known hosts only (per Lesson 6)

```hcl
resource "azurerm_mssql_firewall_rule" "shir_host" {
  name             = "allow-shir-host"
  server_id        = azurerm_mssql_server.primary.id
  start_ip_address = var.shir_vm_public_ip
  end_ip_address   = var.shir_vm_public_ip
}

resource "azurerm_mssql_firewall_rule" "corporate_range" {
  name             = "allow-thornridge-corporate"
  server_id        = azurerm_mssql_server.primary.id
  start_ip_address = "203.0.113.0"
  end_ip_address   = "203.0.113.255"
}
```

Note what's absent: no rule allowing `0.0.0.0`-`255.255.255.255`, and `Allow Azure services` is left off -- both deliberate, matching the deny-by-default plan from Lesson 6.

## Step 6 -- Variables, so nothing is hardcoded by accident

```hcl
variable "aad_dba_group_object_id" {
  type        = string
  description = "Object ID of the Azure AD group administering PolicyClaimsDB"
}

variable "shir_vm_public_ip" {
  type        = string
  description = "Static outbound IP of the Self-Hosted IR VM used for migration"
}
```

Both values are environment-specific and genuinely variable between non-prod and prod, which is exactly the signal that they belong in `variables.tf` with values supplied per environment, not typed directly into the resource blocks above.

## Step 7 -- Plan, review, apply

```bash
terraform init
terraform plan -out=tfplan
# Review the plan output line by line: exactly 1 resource group,
# 1 server, 1 database, 2 firewall rules -- nothing extra, nothing
# missing, and nothing marked for destruction on a brand-new apply.
terraform apply tfplan
```

Reviewing a plan before approving an apply is not a formality on a database about to hold real policyholder data -- it's the last point where a typo in a CIDR range, an accidentally-omitted `zone_redundant`, or a stray resource pulled in by a bad copy-paste gets caught before it's live, rather than discovered afterward during an audit.

## Step 8 -- Verify the real thing exists

```bash
az sql db show \
  --resource-group rg-thornridge-sql-prod \
  --server thornridge-sql-server \
  --name PolicyClaimsDB \
  --query "{status:status, zoneRedundant:zoneRedundant}"
```

Confirm `status` is `Online` and `zoneRedundant` is `true` -- the database exists, empty, secured, and exactly matching three lessons of planning. Nothing has been migrated into it yet; that's next.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Provisioned the real infrastructure via Terraform: resource group, the primary logical server with Azure AD-only administration -- no SQL admin login created at all -- and PolicyClaimsDB on a zone-redundant General Purpose tier, with firewall rules locked to exactly the SHIR host and our corporate IP range. Every setting traces back to a decision from the last three planning lessons; nothing here was invented on the fly.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: The actual Azure SQL environment now exists, built from code rather than manual portal clicks, which means we have a reviewable, repeatable record of exactly how it's configured. It matches the security and resilience decisions we already walked through and signed off on -- nothing new was introduced during the build itself.
workplaceExplanation.executive: The new database environment is now live in Azure, built to the security and reliability plan we already agreed on -- not assembled ad hoc. It's empty and ready; the actual data migration is the next step.

lessons.title: Migrating the Database With Data Factory
lessons.summary: Executing the real on-prem-to-Azure migration with ADF — bulk load, incremental sync, and the cutover runbook that finally retires the on-prem database.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding: This lesson runs the actual migration: the ADF pipeline `pl_migrate_policyclaims` performing the initial bulk Copy Activity load of Thornridge's on-prem `PolicyClaimsDB` tables through the Self-Hosted Integration Runtime, followed by a watermark-based incremental sync that keeps the Azure SQL copy converging toward the live on-prem data, and finally the scripted cutover runbook that freezes writes, runs one last sync, verifies the data, and repoints the claims-processing app at Azure.
lessons.explainSimple: Imagine moving a busy store's cash register records to a new building while the old store stays open. You don't just grab everything once and call it done — you copy everything first, then keep copying just the new sales every few minutes so both registers stay almost in sync, and only for a few minutes at the very end do you briefly stop ringing anything up, copy the last few sales, and flip the sign to the new building.
lessons.explainProfessional: This is a minimal-downtime migration pattern built on Azure Data Factory's Copy Activity and a Self-Hosted Integration Runtime for on-prem connectivity, using a watermark (high-water-mark) incremental load strategy rather than a single big-bang copy. The initial full load establishes a starting point; the recurring delta sync, filtered on a last-modified column and tracked in a dedicated watermark table, narrows the gap between the two databases down to minutes instead of days. Cutover is the one moment the pattern can't automate away — a short, scripted freeze window where writes stop, one final delta sync closes the remaining gap, and row-count and checksum verification happens before the application is repointed, so 'the migration is done' is a verified claim and not an assumption.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 — Confirm the on-prem-to-Azure connectivity path is live

Before anything moves, confirm the Self-Hosted Integration Runtime (SHIR) registered against the `thornridge-adf` Data Factory instance is actually reachable from Thornridge's on-prem network and reporting healthy:

```bash
az datafactory integration-runtime list \
  --resource-group rg-thornridge-sql-prod \
  --factory-name thornridge-adf \
  --output table
```

Confirm `shir-thornridge-onprem` shows `Status: Online` with at least one registered node. This is the only path traffic takes between Thornridge's on-prem SQL Server and Azure — the Copy Activity below cannot reach the source without it.

## Step 2 — Build the linked services

Two linked services, one per side of the move:

```json
{
  "name": "LS_OnPrem_PolicyClaims",
  "properties": {
    "type": "SqlServer",
    "typeProperties": {
      "connectionString": "Server=THORN-SQL01;Database=PolicyClaimsDB;User ID=adf_svc;Password=***"
    },
    "connectVia": { "referenceName": "shir-thornridge-onprem", "type": "IntegrationRuntimeReference" }
  }
}
```

```json
{
  "name": "LS_AzureSql_PolicyClaimsDB",
  "properties": {
    "type": "AzureSqlDatabase",
    "typeProperties": {
      "connectionString": "Server=tcp:thornridge-sql-server.database.windows.net,1433;Database=PolicyClaimsDB;Authentication=Active Directory Service Principal;..."
    }
  }
}
```

## Step 3 — pl_migrate_policyclaims: the bulk initial load

The pipeline's first branch is a one-time full Copy Activity per table, driven by a Lookup against a table list rather than one hardcoded activity per table:

```
Lookup (GetTableList) -> ForEach (table in list) -> Copy Activity
  Source: LS_OnPrem_PolicyClaims, query: SELECT * FROM [{table}]
  Sink:   LS_AzureSql_PolicyClaimsDB, table [{table}], Copy method: Bulk insert
```

Run this once, overnight, with the on-prem database still fully live and being written to by the claims-processing app — this is the baseline copy; it will already be stale by the time it finishes for a database this size.

## Step 4 — The incremental sync that keeps both databases in step

A watermark table tracks the last-synced point per table:

```sql
CREATE TABLE dbo.WatermarkTable (
    TableName       NVARCHAR(256) NOT NULL PRIMARY KEY,
    WatermarkValue  DATETIME2     NOT NULL
);

INSERT INTO dbo.WatermarkTable (TableName, WatermarkValue)
VALUES ('Policies', '1900-01-01'), ('Claims', '1900-01-01');
```

The pipeline's second branch runs on a 15-minute trigger: a Lookup reads the old watermark, a second Lookup computes `SELECT MAX(ModifiedDate) FROM Claims` as the new watermark, a Copy Activity pulls only the delta (`WHERE ModifiedDate > @oldWatermark AND ModifiedDate <= @newWatermark`) into a staging table, a Stored Procedure activity upserts (`MERGE`) staging into the real Azure SQL table, and a final activity writes the new watermark back. This is what keeps the Azure copy converging toward current state without ever re-copying the whole table.

## Step 5 — The cutover runbook

Cutover is a short, scripted sequence, not a vague "flip it over":

1. Announce the freeze window to the app team and schedule it for off-hours.
2. Revoke write permissions on the on-prem database (`REVOKE INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE ON SCHEMA::dbo TO app_role`) so no new writes can occur during the freeze.
3. Trigger one final, manual run of the incremental sync pipeline to pull the last few minutes of changes:
```bash
az datafactory pipeline create-run \
  --resource-group rg-thornridge-sql-prod \
  --factory-name thornridge-adf \
  --name pl_migrate_policyclaims
```
4. Verify row counts and an aggregate checksum match between the two databases for every migrated table before declaring the data trustworthy:
```sql
SELECT COUNT(*) AS row_count, CHECKSUM_AGG(CHECKSUM(*)) AS table_checksum FROM dbo.Claims;
```
5. Repoint the claims-processing app's connection string to `thornridge-sql-server.database.windows.net` and restart the app tier.
6. Re-enable writes and run a short smoke test (create a test claim, confirm it lands in Azure SQL) before closing the freeze window.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: The initial bulk load for all PolicyClaimsDB tables is complete via pl_migrate_policyclaims, and the 15-minute watermark-based incremental sync is running and keeping Azure SQL within roughly 15-20 minutes of the on-prem source. The cutover runbook is written and dry-run tested end-to-end; ready to schedule the real freeze window.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: The database move itself is underway without taking the current system offline — we're running both databases in parallel and syncing every 15 minutes, so the actual cutover is a short, scheduled freeze window instead of a weekend-long outage.
workplaceExplanation.executive: We're moving the policy and claims database to Azure without extended downtime. The old and new systems stay in sync automatically until we do a short, planned switch-over, so the business keeps running normally right up to cutover.

lessons.title: Hardening Security: TDE, Azure AD Auth, and Auditing
lessons.summary: Real T-SQL and Azure CLI to confirm TDE, move the claims-processing app off a SQL login onto Azure AD authentication, and turn on SQL Auditing to a storage account.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding: This lesson hardens PolicyClaimsDB's security posture with three concrete, verifiable changes: confirming Transparent Data Encryption is actually active rather than assumed, replacing the claims-processing app's SQL login with an Azure AD-based contained database user tied to its own identity, and turning on SQL Auditing so every query against this database writes a verifiable record to a dedicated storage account.
lessons.explainSimple: Think of three separate locks on a filing cabinet full of sensitive insurance records: one that scrambles the files themselves so they're useless if someone steals the whole cabinet, one that makes sure only people with their own verified ID badge can open it instead of a shared key anyone could copy, and one that keeps a logbook of exactly who opened the cabinet and when. This lesson checks and turns on all three.
lessons.explainProfessional: These three controls map to distinct threat models an insurer's auditors will ask about by name: TDE protects data at rest against someone obtaining the physical database files or a backup; Azure AD authentication replaces a static SQL login and password — a shared secret that can leak into source control or a config file — with per-identity, centrally revocable access tied to Azure AD's own conditional access and MFA policies; and SQL Auditing produces an immutable, timestamped record of who queried what, which is the artifact a compliance review or a breach investigation actually needs. None of these are exotic Azure features — they're the baseline expectation for a database holding policyholder PII and claims data, and this lesson treats each one as something to verify with a query or a CLI call, not something to assume is 'probably on.'
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 — Confirm TDE is active on PolicyClaimsDB

Azure SQL Database turns on Transparent Data Encryption by default, but confirm it rather than assume it, especially after a migration:

```sql
SELECT
    db.name AS database_name,
    dek.encryption_state,
    CASE dek.encryption_state WHEN 3 THEN 'Encrypted' ELSE 'Not Encrypted' END AS encryption_state_desc,
    dek.encryptor_type,
    dek.encryption_scan_state_desc
FROM sys.dm_database_encryption_keys dek
JOIN sys.databases db ON dek.database_id = db.database_id
WHERE db.name = 'PolicyClaimsDB';
```

`encryption_state = 3` is encrypted. Capture this result in the migration sign-off — a regional insurer's claims data is exactly the kind of PII/PHI-adjacent data an auditor will ask to see this proof for.

## Step 2 — Set an Azure AD admin on the logical server

Azure AD authentication requires an Azure AD admin configured at the server level first:

```bash
az sql server ad-admin create \
  --resource-group rg-thornridge-sql-prod \
  --server thornridge-sql-server \
  --display-name "Thornridge SQL Admins" \
  --object-id <aad-group-object-id>
```

## Step 3 — Replace the app's SQL login with an Azure AD contained database user

Connect to PolicyClaimsDB as the Azure AD admin and create a contained user mapped to the claims-processing app's Azure AD service principal, instead of a SQL login with a password sitting in a config file:

```sql
CREATE USER [sp-claims-processing-app] FROM EXTERNAL PROVIDER;

ALTER ROLE db_datareader ADD MEMBER [sp-claims-processing-app];
ALTER ROLE db_datawriter ADD MEMBER [sp-claims-processing-app];
```

Once the app is validated against this user, drop the legacy SQL login it used before the migration:

```sql
DROP USER IF EXISTS [legacy_claims_sql_login];
```

## Step 4 — Turn on SQL Auditing against a dedicated storage account

```bash
az storage account create \
  --name thornridgesqlaudit \
  --resource-group rg-thornridge-sql-prod \
  --location eastus2 \
  --sku Standard_LRS \
  --min-tls-version TLS1_2

az sql db audit-policy update \
  --resource-group rg-thornridge-sql-prod \
  --server thornridge-sql-server \
  --name PolicyClaimsDB \
  --state Enabled \
  --storage-account thornridgesqlaudit \
  --retention-days 90
```

## Step 5 — Confirm the audit policy is actually capturing events

```bash
az sql db audit-policy show \
  --resource-group rg-thornridge-sql-prod \
  --server thornridge-sql-server \
  --name PolicyClaimsDB
```

Then run one deliberate test query against PolicyClaimsDB and confirm an audit log blob appears in the `thornridgesqlaudit` storage account's `sqldbauditlogs` container within a few minutes — auditing that's "enabled" but never verified to actually be writing logs is a false sense of security.

## Step 6 — Document the three controls as a single compliance artifact

Treat the TDE confirmation, the Azure AD cutover, and the audit policy as one artifact handed to compliance, not three separate checkboxes buried in different tickets. Thornridge's InfoSec team will eventually ask "show me that PolicyClaimsDB is encrypted, that the application isn't authenticating with a shared password, and that we can prove who queried what, going back ninety days" — and the right answer is three dated query outputs and CLI results sitting in one migration sign-off document, not three different engineers' memories of having done it at some point during the migration. Note explicitly in that document which legacy SQL logins were dropped and on what date, since "we moved to Azure AD auth" is a much weaker claim than "we moved to Azure AD auth, and here is proof the old SQL login no longer exists."

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: TDE is confirmed active on PolicyClaimsDB (encryption_state = 3). The claims-processing app now authenticates as the Azure AD service principal sp-claims-processing-app via a contained database user, and the legacy SQL login has been dropped.
