SQL Auditing is enabled against the thornridgesqlaudit storage account with a 90-day retention, and I ran a test query to confirm audit log blobs are actually landing, not just that the policy shows 'Enabled.'
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: Three concrete security controls are now in place and verified on PolicyClaimsDB: data is encrypted at rest, the application no longer relies on a shared password, and every query against this database is now logged for audit purposes. This is standard due diligence for a database holding policyholder and claims data.
workplaceExplanation.executive: The new database for policy and claims data is encrypted, the application connects using its own verified identity instead of a shared password, and every access to this data is now logged. These are the baseline protections an insurance regulator or auditor will expect to see.

lessons.title: Setting Up Active Geo-Replication and a Failover Group
lessons.summary: The most important lesson in this phase: active geo-replication and an auto-failover group with a stable listener endpoint — and the one assumption this lesson explicitly does not verify.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding: This lesson builds Thornridge's disaster-recovery backbone for PolicyClaimsDB: a secondary Azure SQL logical server in a different Azure region, Active Geo-Replication keeping it continuously synchronized with the primary, and an auto-failover group — `thornridge-sql-failover-group` — wrapping both servers behind one stable listener endpoint so a regional outage can fail over automatically instead of waiting on a manual, middle-of-the-night intervention.
lessons.explainSimple: Imagine a backup copy of an important filing cabinet kept in a different building across town, updated continuously so it's never more than a few seconds behind the original. If the first building loses power, you don't want everyone trying to remember a different address for the backup cabinet — you want one sign on the door that always points to whichever cabinet is currently the real one, automatically. That sign is the failover group's listener. What we can't check from here is whether everyone who uses the filing cabinet is actually reading the sign, or whether some of them wrote down the first building's address by hand and never updated it.
lessons.explainProfessional: Active Geo-Replication provides asynchronous, continuous replication to a secondary in a different region; wrapping it in an auto-failover group adds automatic health detection, a configurable grace period before failover triggers, and — critically — a stable DNS endpoint (the listener) that abstracts away which server is currently primary. The entire value of that listener depends on every client actually connecting through it instead of hardcoding the primary server's name. That's a client-side configuration detail, owned by whichever team builds the connecting application, and it is invisible from the database or infrastructure side — Azure has no way to inspect an application's connection string and confirm it uses the listener. This lesson builds the Azure side correctly and completely, and is explicit that the application-side assumption is exactly that: an assumption, not a verified fact, until a real failover test or an app-team connection-string audit confirms it.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 — Provision the secondary logical server

The primary server and PolicyClaimsDB were provisioned by Terraform in Lesson 8. The secondary server, and the failover group wrapping it, are set up here directly with Azure CLI so the exact replication and failover behavior can be inspected step by step before it gets folded back into Terraform state:

```bash
az sql server create \
  --name thornridge-sql-server-secondary \
  --resource-group rg-thornridge-sql-prod \
  --location centralus \
  --admin-user thornridgeadmin \
  --admin-password "<secure-password>"
```

`thornridge-sql-server` lives in East US 2; the secondary is deliberately placed in Central US — a different Azure region — since geo-replication that stays in the same region doesn't protect against a regional outage.

## Step 2 — Add PolicyClaimsDB as a geo-replicated secondary

Either the direct T-SQL form, run against the primary:

```sql
ALTER DATABASE PolicyClaimsDB
ADD SECONDARY ON SERVER [thornridge-sql-server-secondary]
WITH (ALLOW_CONNECTIONS = ALL);
```

or the equivalent Azure CLI form used here for consistency with the rest of this lesson's scripting:

```bash
az sql db replica create \
  --resource-group rg-thornridge-sql-prod \
  --server thornridge-sql-server \
  --name PolicyClaimsDB \
  --partner-server thornridge-sql-server-secondary \
  --partner-resource-group rg-thornridge-sql-prod \
  --secondary-type Geo
```

Confirm the secondary is seeding and then synchronized:

```sql
SELECT role_desc, replication_state_desc, link_type_desc
FROM sys.dm_database_replica_states;
```

## Step 3 — Wrap it in an auto-failover group

Active Geo-Replication alone requires a manual failover call; the failover group is what adds automatic detection and a stable connection endpoint:

```bash
az sql failover-group create \
  --name thornridge-sql-failover-group \
  --partner-server thornridge-sql-server-secondary \
  --resource-group rg-thornridge-sql-prod \
  --server thornridge-sql-server \
  --add-db PolicyClaimsDB \
  --failover-policy Automatic \
  --grace-period 1
```

`--grace-period 1` gives Azure one hour of sustained primary unavailability before it fails over automatically — long enough to rule out a transient blip, short enough to matter for an insurer's claims-processing SLA.

## Step 4 — Confirm the listener endpoint

```bash
az sql failover-group show \
  --name thornridge-sql-failover-group \
  --resource-group rg-thornridge-sql-prod \
  --server thornridge-sql-server \
  --query "{readWriteEndpoint:readWriteEndpoint, readOnlyEndpoint:readOnlyEndpoint, replicationRole:replicationRole}"
```

The read-write listener is `thornridge-sql-failover-group.database.windows.net` — this is the hostname that is supposed to survive a failover, automatically redirecting to whichever server is currently primary, without anyone touching DNS or a config file by hand.

## Step 5 — State the gap this lesson leaves, in writing

The Azure-side configuration here is complete and correct: active geo-replication from `thornridge-sql-server`/`PolicyClaimsDB` to `thornridge-sql-server-secondary`, wrapped in `thornridge-sql-failover-group`, with a working listener endpoint. What this lesson has not done, and cannot do from the database side, is confirm that the claims-processing application — owned and configured by the app team, not by this database build — actually connects using `thornridge-sql-failover-group.database.windows.net` rather than `thornridge-sql-server.database.windows.net` directly. We've configured the failover group correctly; whether every application that connects to this database is actually using the listener endpoint, rather than the server name directly, is a question for the app team, or for a real failover test, not something Terraform or Azure can enforce from the database side. That assumption goes into the migration runbook as an open item, not a confirmed fact.

## Step 6 — Decide what gets folded back into Terraform, and what doesn't

The secondary server and failover group were built here with Azure CLI, step by step, so the replication and failover behavior could be inspected directly rather than taken on faith from a plan file. Before calling this lesson done, bring `thornridge-sql-server-secondary` and `thornridge-sql-failover-group` into the same Terraform state that provisioned the primary in Lesson 8 — otherwise a future `terraform apply` has no record of these resources and could propose to recreate or orphan them. Importing both resources (`terraform import`) and confirming `terraform plan` shows zero drift against what was just built by hand is the step that keeps this disaster-recovery setup from silently falling out of the infrastructure-as-code story the rest of this project is telling.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Active geo-replication and the auto-failover group are live: thornridge-sql-server-secondary in Central US, thornridge-sql-failover-group wrapping PolicyClaimsDB with an Automatic failover policy and a one-hour grace period. The listener endpoint thornridge-sql-failover-group.database.windows.net is confirmed reachable and correctly routing to the current primary. One open item I'm flagging, not closing myself: I have not verified the claims-processing app's own connection string points at the listener rather than the server name directly — that's the app team's configuration, and it needs a real failover test to confirm.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: Our failover protection is built and verified on the database side — if the primary region has a real outage, the secondary can take over automatically. One dependency I'm flagging for the app team: they need to confirm their connection string targets the failover group's listener address, not the primary server directly, or a failover won't actually route their traffic.
workplaceExplanation.executive: If our primary data center has a serious outage, the system is built to switch automatically to a backup copy in a different region. The database side of that protection is fully in place and tested; we still need the application team to confirm their software is actually set up to follow that switch when it happens.

lessons.title: Establishing a Performance Baseline With Query Store
lessons.summary: Enabling and tuning Query Store, running a representative workload, and freezing the first performance baseline this project will be measured against.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding: This lesson establishes the performance baseline the rest of the project gets compared against: confirming Query Store is enabled and tuned for a transactional claims workload, running PolicyClaimsDB through a representative day of real traffic, and capturing the actual top resource-consuming queries — by duration, CPU, and logical reads — into a preserved snapshot table.
lessons.explainSimple: Before you try to make a car faster, you time how fast it currently goes around the track — otherwise you have no way to know if your changes actually helped. This lesson is that first timed lap for the new database: we turn on the car's own built-in stopwatch, drive it through a normal day exactly the way the business actually uses it, and write down exactly which parts of the drive took the longest.
lessons.explainProfessional: Query Store is Azure SQL's built-in query performance repository — it persists query text, execution plans, and runtime statistics across restarts, which is what makes a before/after performance comparison possible at all instead of relying on a developer's point-in-time impression. The baseline's value depends entirely on capturing it against a representative workload; a baseline captured against an idle or synthetic database measures nothing real. Pulling the top queries by three different metrics — duration, CPU, and logical I/O — matters because the query that's slowest in wall-clock time and the query that's most expensive in CPU or I/O are frequently different queries, and a service-tier or indexing decision made from only one of those three views can miss the real bottleneck. Freezing the result into a dedicated, dated table turns this from a one-time look into a durable artifact every later tuning claim gets checked against.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 — Confirm Query Store is on, and set capture options deliberately

Azure SQL Database enables Query Store by default, but confirm the operation mode and capture settings rather than assume the defaults fit a transactional claims workload:

```sql
SELECT actual_state_desc, desired_state_desc, query_capture_mode_desc,
       max_storage_size_mb, current_storage_size_mb, interval_length_minutes
FROM sys.database_query_store_options;
```

If it's off, or capturing too narrowly:

```sql
ALTER DATABASE PolicyClaimsDB SET QUERY_STORE = ON;

ALTER DATABASE PolicyClaimsDB SET QUERY_STORE (
    OPERATION_MODE = READ_WRITE,
    QUERY_CAPTURE_MODE = AUTO,
    MAX_STORAGE_SIZE_MB = 2048,
    INTERVAL_LENGTH_MINUTES = 15,
    STALE_QUERY_THRESHOLD_DAYS = 30
);
```

`QUERY_CAPTURE_MODE = AUTO` skips one-off ad hoc queries and focuses storage on the queries the claims-processing app actually repeats — exactly the ones a baseline needs.

## Step 2 — Run a representative baseline workload

A baseline captured against an empty, idle database is worthless. Run PolicyClaimsDB through a normal business cycle before capturing anything — a full day of real claims-processing traffic (policy lookups, claim status updates, the nightly batch job that recalculates premium adjustments) covers the actual query mix this baseline needs to reflect. For a pre-production dry run, replay a representative sample of production traffic against the Azure SQL copy using the application's own test harness rather than hand-written synthetic queries, since Query Store's value depends on seeing real query shapes and real parameter skew.

## Step 3 — Pull the top resource-consuming queries

```sql
SELECT TOP 20
    q.query_id,
    qt.query_sql_text,
    rs.avg_duration / 1000.0        AS avg_duration_ms,
    rs.avg_cpu_time / 1000.0         AS avg_cpu_time_ms,
    rs.avg_logical_io_reads,
    rs.count_executions
FROM sys.query_store_query q
JOIN sys.query_store_query_text qt
    ON q.query_text_id = qt.query_text_id
JOIN sys.query_store_plan p
    ON q.query_id = p.query_id
JOIN sys.query_store_runtime_stats rs
    ON p.plan_id = rs.plan_id
JOIN sys.query_store_runtime_stats_interval rsi
    ON rs.runtime_stats_interval_id = rsi.runtime_stats_interval_id
WHERE rsi.start_time >= DATEADD(DAY, -1, SYSUTCDATETIME())
ORDER BY rs.avg_duration DESC;
```

Run the same query ordered by `avg_cpu_time` and separately by `avg_logical_io_reads` — the worst query by duration and the worst query by CPU are not always the same query, and both matter for sizing the service tier correctly.

## Step 4 — Freeze this result as the baseline, not a one-time look

A baseline only has value if it's preserved somewhere comparisons can be run against later:

```sql
SELECT
    q.query_id, qt.query_sql_text,
    rs.avg_duration, rs.avg_cpu_time, rs.avg_logical_io_reads, rs.count_executions,
    SYSUTCDATETIME() AS captured_at
INTO dbo.PerfBaseline_20261023
FROM sys.query_store_query q
JOIN sys.query_store_query_text qt ON q.query_text_id = qt.query_text_id
JOIN sys.query_store_plan p ON q.query_id = p.query_id
JOIN sys.query_store_runtime_stats rs ON p.plan_id = rs.plan_id
JOIN sys.query_store_runtime_stats_interval rsi ON rs.runtime_stats_interval_id = rsi.runtime_stats_interval_id
WHERE rsi.start_time >= DATEADD(DAY, -1, SYSUTCDATETIME());
```

## Step 5 — Write down what this baseline is for

This captured snapshot — `dbo.PerfBaseline_20261023` plus the exported top-20 report — is the number every future performance claim gets checked against. When a future change (an index, a query rewrite, a service-tier resize) claims to have improved performance, the honest proof is the same Query Store query run again and compared against this exact baseline, not a developer's impression that "it feels faster."

## Step 6 — Treat one day of data as a starting point, not the final word

A single day's capture is enough to start tuning conversations, but insurance claims traffic has real seasonality — month-end premium billing runs, and a spike in claim submissions after a regional storm event, both produce a very different query mix than an ordinary Tuesday. Plan to re-run Steps 3 and 4 after a full billing cycle and keep both snapshots (`dbo.PerfBaseline_20261023` and a follow-up capture) side by side rather than overwriting the first one. A query that looks fine against one day's baseline can be the actual bottleneck once a realistic monthly cycle, including its peak days, is accounted for.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Query Store is confirmed on and configured (AUTO capture, 15-minute intervals, 2GB cap). Ran PolicyClaimsDB through a full day of representative claims-processing traffic and captured the top 20 queries by duration, CPU, and logical reads into dbo.PerfBaseline_20261023. This is the number set any future tuning work gets measured against.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: We now have a documented, data-backed snapshot of how the system performs today, captured from a real day of claims-processing activity, not a guess. Any future performance work will be judged against this specific baseline instead of a subjective 'it feels faster.'
workplaceExplanation.executive: Before anything else changes, we've recorded exactly how fast the new system runs today, using real usage data. That gives us an honest way to measure whether future improvements actually make a difference, instead of relying on impressions.

lessons.title: Automating Maintenance With PowerShell and Azure Automation
lessons.summary: Building three scheduled PowerShell runbooks in Azure Automation -- fragmentation-driven index maintenance, an integrity check, and a real backup-restore verification -- so routine database health work runs itself.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
Thornridge's claims database now has a correct DR setup, encryption, and a migrated schema -- but day-to-day health still depends entirely on someone remembering to check index fragmentation, run an integrity check, and confirm backups actually restore. This lesson builds that memory into the platform itself: a dedicated Azure Automation Account, `thornridge-automation`, running three PowerShell runbooks on fixed schedules -- one that rebuilds or reorganizes indexes based on real fragmentation thresholds, one that runs `DBCC CHECKDB` against `PolicyClaimsDB`, and one that proves backups are restorable by actually restoring one to a throwaway database and tearing it down.

None of this is new SQL Server knowledge -- it's the same maintenance tasks any DBA already knows, now running unattended, on a schedule, with a managed identity instead of a stored password, and an alert if any of the three ever fails.
lessons.explainSimple:
Think about a car that needs its oil changed, its tires rotated, and its brakes checked -- all on their own separate schedules. You could try to remember all three dates yourself, but eventually you'll forget one, usually right before it actually mattered. A better fix is a car that reminds itself and does some of the work automatically.

That's what we're building for Thornridge's claims database: three separate maintenance jobs -- tidying up the indexes, checking for hidden damage, and proving the spare tire (the backup) actually works -- all running on their own schedule, with nobody having to remember to kick any of them off by hand.
lessons.explainProfessional:
Scheduled database maintenance is unglamorous, but it's exactly the kind of work that silently stops happening the moment it depends on a person's memory rather than a schedule -- and the gap is usually invisible until a fragmented index tanks a query plan or a backup turns out to be unrestorable during an actual emergency. Azure Automation with a managed identity solves both the "did anyone run this" problem and the "is there a password sitting in a script somewhere" problem at once: the runbook authenticates as its own Azure AD identity against `PolicyClaimsDB`, scoped to exactly the permissions each job needs, with nothing resembling a credential checked into source control.

The backup-verification runbook is the one most teams skip, and it's the one that matters most: a backup that has never actually been restored is a hope, not a guarantee. Performing a real point-in-time restore to a disposable database on a schedule, checking it for real rows, and tearing it down is the only way to know Thornridge's recovery point objective is actually achievable, rather than assumed.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 — Stand up the Automation Account and give it a scoped identity

Create a dedicated Azure Automation Account, `thornridge-automation`, in `rg-thornridge-sql-prod`, and turn on a system-assigned managed identity instead of storing a SQL login and password inside a runbook:

```powershell
az automation account create `
  --name thornridge-automation `
  --resource-group rg-thornridge-sql-prod `
  --location eastus2

az automation account identity assign `
  --name thornridge-automation `
  --resource-group rg-thornridge-sql-prod
```

Grant that identity exactly the access it needs -- `db_owner` on `PolicyClaimsDB` is overkill; a dedicated user mapped to the managed identity, with `db_ddladmin` membership and `VIEW DATABASE STATE`, is enough for index maintenance and integrity checks:

```sql
CREATE USER [thornridge-automation] FROM EXTERNAL PROVIDER;
ALTER ROLE db_ddladmin ADD MEMBER [thornridge-automation];
GRANT VIEW DATABASE STATE TO [thornridge-automation];
```

## Step 2 — Build the index-maintenance runbook

Fragmentation decisions should be data-driven, not a blind weekly `REBUILD ALL` -- that wastes compute on indexes that don't need it and can bloat the transaction log. `Rebuild-Or-Reorganize-Indexes` queries `sys.dm_db_index_physical_stats` and picks the action per the standard thresholds: reorganize between 10% and 30% fragmentation, rebuild above 30%:

```powershell
Connect-AzAccount -Identity | Out-Null
$token = (Get-AzAccessToken -ResourceUrl "https://database.windows.net/").Token

$frag = Invoke-Sqlcmd -ServerInstance "thornridge-sql-server.database.windows.net" `
  -Database "PolicyClaimsDB" -AccessToken $token -Query @"
SELECT s.name AS schema_name, t.name AS table_name, i.name AS index_name,
       ips.avg_fragmentation_in_percent
FROM sys.dm_db_index_physical_stats(DB_ID(), NULL, NULL, NULL, 'LIMITED') ips
JOIN sys.indexes i ON ips.object_id = i.object_id AND ips.index_id = i.index_id
JOIN sys.tables t ON i.object_id = t.object_id
JOIN sys.schemas s ON t.schema_id = s.schema_id
WHERE ips.page_count > 1000 AND i.name IS NOT NULL
"@

foreach ($row in $frag) {
  $action = if ($row.avg_fragmentation_in_percent -ge 30) { "REBUILD" }
            elseif ($row.avg_fragmentation_in_percent -ge 10) { "REORGANIZE" }
            else { $null }
  if ($action) {
    Invoke-Sqlcmd -ServerInstance "thornridge-sql-server.database.windows.net" -Database "PolicyClaimsDB" `
      -AccessToken $token -QueryTimeout 1800 `
      -Query "ALTER INDEX [$($row.index_name)] ON [$($row.schema_name)].[$($row.table_name)] $action;"
  }
}
```

## Step 3 — Build the integrity-check runbook

`Check-PolicyClaimsDB-Integrity` runs `DBCC CHECKDB` and treats any non-clean result as a failure, not a log line:

```powershell
Connect-AzAccount -Identity | Out-Null
$token = (Get-AzAccessToken -ResourceUrl "https://database.windows.net/").Token
try {
  Invoke-Sqlcmd -ServerInstance "thornridge-sql-server.database.windows.net" -Database "PolicyClaimsDB" `
    -AccessToken $token -QueryTimeout 3600 `
    -Query "DBCC CHECKDB ('PolicyClaimsDB') WITH NO_INFOMSGS, ALL_ERRORMSGS;"
} catch {
  throw "DBCC CHECKDB reported a problem on PolicyClaimsDB: $_"
}
```

A failed runbook run fires Azure Monitor's built-in Automation alert, routed to the same alert action group the failover group already uses.

## Step 4 — Build the backup-verification runbook

The only backup worth trusting is one that's actually been restored. `Verify-PolicyClaimsDB-Backup` performs a real point-in-time restore to a throwaway database, checks it for data, then tears it down:

```powershell
Connect-AzAccount -Identity | Out-Null
$testDb = "PolicyClaimsDB_RestoreTest_$(Get-Date -Format yyyyMMddHHmm)"

Restore-AzSqlDatabase -FromPointInTimeBackup -PointInTime (Get-Date).AddMinutes(-15) `
  -ResourceGroupName "rg-thornridge-sql-prod" -ServerName "thornridge-sql-server" `
  -TargetDatabaseName $testDb `
  -ResourceId "/subscriptions/<sub-id>/resourceGroups/rg-thornridge-sql-prod/providers/Microsoft.Sql/servers/thornridge-sql-server/databases/PolicyClaimsDB"

$token = (Get-AzAccessToken -ResourceUrl "https://database.windows.net/").Token
$check = Invoke-Sqlcmd -ServerInstance "thornridge-sql-server.database.windows.net" -Database $testDb `
  -AccessToken $token -Query "SELECT COUNT(*) AS cnt FROM dbo.Policies;"
if ($check.cnt -le 0) { throw "Restore test produced zero policy rows -- PITR cannot be trusted." }

Remove-AzSqlDatabase -ResourceGroupName "rg-thornridge-sql-prod" -ServerName "thornridge-sql-server" -DatabaseName $testDb -Force
```

## Step 5 — Schedule all three and connect them to alerting

Index maintenance runs weekly, Sunday 1:00am; integrity checks run nightly at 2:30am; backup verification runs monthly, first Sunday 3:00am -- each on its own Automation schedule, each failure routed to the same alert action group the DBA team already watches for the failover group itself. Nothing here replaces a human reviewing the logs periodically -- it replaces a human having to remember to run any of this by hand.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Stood up thornridge-automation with a managed identity instead of embedded SQL credentials, and built three runbooks: fragmentation-driven index maintenance against sys.dm_db_index_physical_stats, a DBCC CHECKDB integrity check, and a backup-verification runbook that actually performs a point-in-time restore to a throwaway database rather than trusting that backups exist. Scheduled weekly, nightly, and monthly respectively, all wired to the same alert action group as the failover group.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: Routine database maintenance -- index health, integrity checks, and proving backups actually restore -- now runs on its own schedule instead of depending on someone remembering to do it. Any failure in any of the three jobs raises an alert automatically.
workplaceExplanation.executive: We've automated the maintenance work that keeps the claims database healthy and its backups trustworthy, so it happens on a fixed schedule rather than depending on someone's memory, and we get alerted immediately if any of it doesn't run cleanly.

lessons.title: Setting Up CI/CD for Schema Changes
lessons.summary: Version-controlling PolicyClaimsDB's schema in a SQL Server Database Project and wiring GitHub Actions to build, dry-run, and publish the DACPAC, with a required human review of the pre-deployment script before anything reaches production.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
`PolicyClaimsDB`'s schema has existed only as whatever state the live Azure SQL Database happens to be in -- changes get made by hand, with no record of who changed what, or why, until something breaks and nobody can say what changed last. This lesson fixes that at the root: the schema moves into a Git-versioned SQL Server Database Project, and a GitHub Actions pipeline builds it into a `PolicyClaimsDB.dacpac`, runs a pre-deployment dry run that a person has to actually review, and only then publishes the real change -- on merge to `main`, never before.

This is the same discipline application code already gets at Thornridge -- a reviewed pull request, an automated build, a gate before production -- applied to the one part of the system that used to skip all of it: the database schema itself.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine if your house's blueprint lived only in the contractor's head, and every time something got changed, nobody wrote it down anywhere. Eventually someone knocks down a wall that was actually load-bearing, and there's no record anyone can check beforehand to catch it.

So instead, we write the blueprint down, in a shared, version-controlled document everyone can see. Before any real wall gets touched, a computer draws up exactly what would change and shows it to a person to approve first -- and only after that approval does the actual change happen.
lessons.explainProfessional:
A DACPAC-based deployment pipeline turns schema changes from something that happens silently against a live database into something that happens through source control, with the same review discipline as application code. The critical safeguard isn't the build step -- `dotnet build` on a `.sqlproj` is mechanical -- it's the pre-deployment dry run, `SqlPackage /Action:Script`, which compares the DACPAC against the actual target database and generates the literal T-SQL that would run, without running it. That script is what a reviewer actually reads before approving a pull request, which is the only point in this whole pipeline where a human can catch an unintended `DROP COLUMN` or data-truncating type change before it happens.

`BlockOnPossibleDataLoss=true` on the real `/Action:Publish` step is the mechanical backstop behind that human review, not a replacement for it -- a reviewer who missed something still gets stopped by the tool itself before data is actually lost. Branch protection making the dry-run review mandatory is what turns this from a nice idea into something that cannot be skipped under deadline pressure.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 — Put the schema in Git, not just in the database

`PolicyClaimsDB`'s schema lives in a SQL Server Database Project, `database/PolicyClaimsDB/PolicyClaimsDB.sqlproj`, checked into the same GitHub repo as the claims-processing application. Every table, index, and stored procedure is a `.sql` file under source control -- a schema change is now a diffable pull request, not an undocumented `ALTER TABLE` run by hand against production.

## Step 2 — Build the DACPAC and run a pre-deployment dry run on every pull request

```yaml
# .github/workflows/schema-cicd.yml
name: PolicyClaimsDB Schema CI/CD
on:
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]
    paths: ["database/PolicyClaimsDB/**"]
  push:
    branches: [main]
    paths: ["database/PolicyClaimsDB/**"]

jobs:
  dry-run:
    if: github.event_name == 'pull_request'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-dotnet@v4
        with: { dotnet-version: "8.0.x" }
      - run: dotnet build database/PolicyClaimsDB/PolicyClaimsDB.sqlproj -c Release
      - run: dotnet tool install -g microsoft.sqlpackage
      - name: Pre-deployment dry run -- generate the script, do NOT apply it
        run: |
          sqlpackage /Action:Script \
            /SourceFile:"database/PolicyClaimsDB/bin/Release/PolicyClaimsDB.dacpac" \
            /TargetConnectionString:"${{ secrets.POLICYCLAIMSDB_CI_CONNECTION }}" \
            /OutputPath:"deploy-preview.sql"
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with: { name: deploy-preview, path: deploy-preview.sql }
```

`/Action:Script` against a CI copy of `PolicyClaimsDB` produces the exact T-SQL the deployment would run -- table alters, index rebuilds, anything SqlPackage thinks is necessary -- without touching a single row. That script becomes a downloadable artifact on the pull request.

## Step 3 — Require a human to actually open that script before merging

A generated dry-run script nobody reads is theater, not a safeguard. The pull-request template adds a checklist item -- "Downloaded and reviewed `deploy-preview.sql`; confirmed no unexpected `DROP` or data-loss operation" -- and branch protection on `main` requires at least one approving review plus the `dry-run` status check before the merge button unlocks. A reviewer who spots an unexpected `DROP COLUMN` in the preview script blocks the PR right there, before it's anywhere near `PolicyClaimsDB`.

## Step 4 — Publish for real on merge to main

```yaml
  publish:
    if: github.event_name == 'push'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: production
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-dotnet@v4
        with: { dotnet-version: "8.0.x" }
      - run: dotnet build database/PolicyClaimsDB/PolicyClaimsDB.sqlproj -c Release
      - run: dotnet tool install -g microsoft.sqlpackage
      - name: Publish to PolicyClaimsDB
        run: |
          sqlpackage /Action:Publish \
            /SourceFile:"database/PolicyClaimsDB/bin/Release/PolicyClaimsDB.dacpac" \
            /TargetConnectionString:"${{ secrets.POLICYCLAIMSDB_PROD_CONNECTION }}" \
            /p:BlockOnPossibleDataLoss=true
```

`BlockOnPossibleDataLoss=true` is not optional here -- it's the mechanical backstop behind the human review in Step 3, so even a reviewer who missed a dangerous change gets stopped by the tool itself.

## Step 5 — Prove the gate actually blocks something

Open a throwaway pull request that drops a column with live data in it. Confirm the dry-run artifact shows the `DROP COLUMN`, confirm a reviewer can catch it in the PR, and confirm that even approving it anyway, `BlockOnPossibleDataLoss` stops `/Action:Publish` from running against production without an explicit override. Revert the change afterward.

## Step 6 — Scope the CI credential so a broken PR can't reach production either

The `POLICYCLAIMSDB_CI_CONNECTION` secret used in Step 2 points at a disposable CI copy of `PolicyClaimsDB`, under a SQL login with `db_owner` on that CI database only -- it has no access to the production server at all. That way, a pull request branch with genuinely broken SQL in it can fail its dry run as badly as it wants without any possibility of reaching anything Thornridge's claims system actually depends on; the blast radius of CI itself is limited to a copy nobody reads from.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: PolicyClaimsDB's schema now lives in a Git-versioned SQL Server Database Project. Every pull request builds the DACPAC and runs a SqlPackage /Action:Script dry run against a CI copy, producing a reviewable deploy script as a PR artifact; branch protection requires a human to review that script before merge. Merges to main rebuild and run /Action:Publish with BlockOnPossibleDataLoss enabled as a mechanical backstop behind the review.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: Every schema change to the claims database now goes through a pull request with an automatic preview of exactly what SQL will run, reviewed by a person before it ships -- no more undocumented changes made by hand against production.
workplaceExplanation.executive: Changes to the claims database's structure now go through the same reviewed, automated process as a software code change -- previewed, approved, then deployed -- instead of someone making a change directly against production.

lessons.title: The Failover Drill Goes Wrong
lessons.summary: A planned failover drill promotes the secondary correctly, but claims-processing starts throwing write errors anyway -- a methodical investigation rules out the database layer and narrows the problem to the application's own connection.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
`thornridge-sql-failover-group` has existed since Lesson 11, correctly built, never once triggered for real. This lesson is the first time anyone actually runs it -- a planned failover drill, scheduled during a maintenance window, meant to prove the disaster-recovery setup works before Thornridge ever needs it to work during a real incident. Instead, the moment the failover completes, claims-processing starts throwing write errors, and the rest of this lesson is a methodical, evidence-based investigation into why -- confirming, one verifiable fact at a time, exactly which layer of the system is actually broken.

By the end, two things are proven, not assumed: Azure's side of the failover group worked exactly as designed, and `PolicyClaimsDB` itself is healthy and fully writable on the new primary. That narrows the entire problem down to one specific place neither of those checks touched -- which is exactly where the next lesson picks up.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine practicing a fire drill for the very first time, years after the building was built, and the fire alarm works perfectly -- but somehow, people still can't find their way out, because nobody ever actually walked the evacuation route before today. The alarm wasn't the problem. Something about how people actually get out was.

That's what happens here. The computer system that's supposed to switch to a backup database during an emergency does exactly what it's supposed to do. But the claims program still can't talk to the database afterward -- so the detective work in this lesson is about figuring out, step by careful step, that the backup database itself is working just fine, which means the real problem has to be somewhere else.
lessons.explainProfessional:
The instinct during an unexpected outage is to start changing things immediately -- fail back, restart the app, anything to make the error stop. That instinct is exactly what this lesson resists in favor of verification: before touching anything, confirm precisely what is and isn't broken, because failing back without understanding the cause just relocates an unknown problem rather than fixing it. The investigation proceeds in a deliberate order that narrows the search space with each step, the same discipline a production incident always rewards over guessing.

First, confirm the orchestration layer: `az sql failover-group show` against both servers confirms the replication roles actually swapped, which rules out a failed or partial failover. Second, confirm the data layer directly, bypassing the application entirely: a hand-run `INSERT` against the new primary succeeds immediately, which rules out corruption, throttling, or an unhealthy database. With both of those layers independently proven healthy, the remaining failure has to live in the one thing neither check touched -- whatever determines which hostname the application itself is actually trying to reach.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 — Run the drill that should have happened months ago

With the failover group built in Lesson 11 and never once tested under real conditions, the DBA team finally schedules a planned failover drill during a Tuesday-morning maintenance window. The command is run against the server currently hosting the secondary, exactly as documented:

```sql
-- Connect to thornridge-sql-server-secondary and run:
ALTER FAILOVER GROUP thornridge-sql-failover-group FAILOVER;
```

This is a planned, synchronous failover -- it should complete with zero data loss, promoting `thornridge-sql-server-secondary` to primary and demoting `thornridge-sql-server` to secondary.

## Step 2 — The alert nobody expected

Within two minutes, the claims-processing application's error dashboard lights up with write failures:

```
[ERROR] SqlException: A network-related or instance-specific error
occurred while establishing a connection to SQL Server. The server
was not found or was not accessible. (thornridge-sql-server.database.windows.net)
```

The instinct to panic and immediately fail back is understandable but wrong -- failing back without understanding the cause just moves the same unknown problem to the other server. The investigation has to answer one question first: is this a database problem, or something else?

## Step 3 — Confirm the Azure side actually did its job

```bash
az sql failover-group show \
  --name thornridge-sql-failover-group \
  --resource-group rg-thornridge-sql-prod \
  --server thornridge-sql-server-secondary \
  --query "{replicationRole:replicationRole, replicationState:replicationState}"
```

```
{
  "replicationRole": "Primary",
  "replicationState": "CATCH_UP"
}
```

`thornridge-sql-server-secondary` reports `Primary`. Checking the other server confirms the mirror image -- `thornridge-sql-server` now reports `Secondary`. A quick look at the geo-replication link status backs this up from the data side too:

```sql
-- Run against thornridge-sql-server-secondary (the new primary)
SELECT partner_server, role_desc, replication_state_desc
FROM sys.dm_geo_replication_link_status;
```

The failover group did exactly what it was built to do: the roles swapped cleanly, with the listener, `thornridge-sql-failover-group.database.windows.net`, now pointed at the new primary. This rules out a failed or partial failover.

## Step 4 — Confirm the database itself is healthy and writable

Connect directly to the new primary -- not through the application, not through the listener yet, just straight to the server that now holds the role -- and prove it accepts writes:

```sql
-- Connect directly to thornridge-sql-server-secondary.database.windows.net
INSERT INTO dbo.ClaimsAuditLog (claim_id, event_type, event_timestamp)
VALUES (999999, 'FAILOVER_DRILL_WRITE_TEST', SYSUTCDATETIME());

SELECT TOP 1 * FROM dbo.ClaimsAuditLog
WHERE event_type = 'FAILOVER_DRILL_WRITE_TEST'
ORDER BY event_timestamp DESC;
```

The insert succeeds immediately and the row reads back. `PolicyClaimsDB` on the new primary is healthy, online, and fully writable right now, by any client that actually connects to it.

## Step 5 — Narrow the gap: it's between the app and the database, not inside either one

Two confirmed facts now bracket the problem precisely: Azure's side failed over correctly, and the database itself accepts writes without issue. Everything that's actually broken has to live in the one place neither check touched -- whatever path the claims-processing application uses to decide which hostname to connect to. That's exactly where the next lesson picks up: reading the application's own configuration instead of anything on the database side.

Clean up the test row before moving on:

```sql
DELETE FROM dbo.ClaimsAuditLog WHERE event_type = 'FAILOVER_DRILL_WRITE_TEST';
```
