Verified the Azure side first -- az sql failover-group show confirms thornridge-sql-server-secondary correctly promoted to Primary -- then verified the database itself by writing directly to the new primary, which succeeded immediately. Both checks rule out a database-layer problem and point squarely at something between the application and the database.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: Our first tested failover drill surfaced a real issue, and we immediately confirmed it is not a database problem -- the database side failed over exactly as designed and is healthy. We've narrowed the cause to the application's connection, and that's what we're tracking down next.
workplaceExplanation.executive: We ran a planned test of our disaster-recovery setup and it surfaced a real gap before a real outage could. The database itself performed correctly during the test; the issue is isolated to how the claims application connects to it, and we're fixing that now.

lessons.title: Finding and Fixing a Connection String That Bypassed the Failover Group
lessons.summary: Tracing the outage to a connection string hardcoded to the primary server's own hostname instead of the failover group's listener, fixing it, proving it with a second drill, and establishing a real recurring tested-failover schedule.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
Lesson 15 proved the failover group and the database itself both worked correctly during the drill. This lesson finds what didn't: the claims-processing application's own connection string, pulled directly from its Azure App Service configuration, hardcoded to `thornridge-sql-server.database.windows.net` -- the primary server's own name -- instead of the failover group's listener, `thornridge-sql-failover-group.database.windows.net`, that Lesson 11 built specifically to survive exactly this situation.

Fixing it is a two-line configuration change. Proving the fix is real takes a second failover drill, watched end to end, confirming the application now survives a failover with zero reconfiguration and zero downtime. The lesson closes by naming the actual root cause honestly: it was never really the connection string -- it was that this entire disaster-recovery setup had gone untested from the day it was built until the moment this incident happened, and that gap gets closed with a real, recurring, scheduled drill going forward.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine you move to a new house and tell everyone your new address -- except you forgot to update the pizza delivery app, which still has your old address saved. Your new house is fine. The delivery service is fine. But the pizza keeps showing up at a house you don't live in anymore, because one app never got the memo about where to actually go.

That's exactly what happened here. The claims program had the old database's address memorized instead of using the one address that was built to always point at whichever database is currently in charge. Fixing it means updating that one saved address -- and then actually testing it again to make sure it works this time.
lessons.explainProfessional:
The root cause is almost embarrassingly small in isolation -- one `Server=` value in one connection string -- which is exactly why it survived undetected since Lesson 11: a code review would have had no reason to flag a connection string that looked perfectly valid and worked fine every single day the primary server stayed the primary server. The bug was latent, not broken, until the one event designed specifically to expose it finally happened.

The fix itself is mechanical: repoint the connection string at the failover group's listener, with `ApplicationIntent=ReadWrite` stated explicitly rather than left to a driver default, since the same failover group also exposes a separate read-only listener that writable traffic must never land on by accident. The verification is what actually closes the incident -- a second drill, run end to end, with the application surviving it without a single configuration change or restart. The honest postmortem conclusion isn't "we fixed a connection string" -- it's that a DR mechanism nobody tests is a DR mechanism nobody can actually trust, which is why this lesson ends by scheduling the drill itself to recur quarterly, not by considering the incident closed.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 — Go straight to the application's own configuration

Lesson 15 proved the database layer is fine. The only remaining place a connection failure can originate is in how the claims-processing application decides what to connect to. It runs as an Azure App Service, `claims-processing-app`, so pull its actual connection string instead of guessing:

```bash
az webapp config connection-string list \
  --name claims-processing-app \
  --resource-group rg-thornridge-sql-prod
```

```json
[
  {
    "name": "PolicyClaimsDb",
    "connectionString": "Server=tcp:thornridge-sql-server.database.windows.net,1433;Database=PolicyClaimsDB;Authentication=Active Directory Managed Identity;Encrypt=True;",
    "type": "SQLAzure"
  }
]
```

There it is. `Server=` points at `thornridge-sql-server.database.windows.net` -- the primary server's own hostname, not the failover group's listener, `thornridge-sql-failover-group.database.windows.net`. When Azure demoted that server to secondary in Lesson 15, every open connection using this string kept trying to reach a server that no longer held the primary role. Azure's automatic client redirection through the listener was never in play, because the app was never configured to use the listener in the first place.

## Step 2 — Confirm it, don't assume it

```sql
-- Run against the connection string's actual target
SELECT @@SERVERNAME, DATABASEPROPERTYEX(DB_NAME(), 'Updateability');
```

Run from a client using the app's exact connection string, this returns `thornridge-sql-server` and `READ_ONLY` -- Azure keeps the demoted former primary online as a readable secondary, which is exactly why the app didn't get a hard connection failure, it got write failures specifically. The application's own exception logs confirm the same thing from the other direction:

```
Msg 3906, Level 16, State 1
Failed to update database "PolicyClaimsDB" because the database
is read-only.
```

Error 3906, not a timeout and not a login failure, is the giveaway: the app successfully reached a real, healthy SQL Server -- just the wrong one for writes. That detail confirms the diagnosis precisely: not a dead server, a wrong target.

## Step 3 — Fix the connection string to point at the listener

```bash
az webapp config connection-string set \
  --name claims-processing-app \
  --resource-group rg-thornridge-sql-prod \
  --settings PolicyClaimsDb="Server=tcp:thornridge-sql-failover-group.database.windows.net,1433;Database=PolicyClaimsDB;Authentication=Active Directory Managed Identity;Encrypt=True;ApplicationIntent=ReadWrite;" \
  --connection-string-type SQLAzure

az webapp restart --name claims-processing-app --resource-group rg-thornridge-sql-prod
```

`ApplicationIntent=ReadWrite` is stated explicitly rather than left to the driver default, because the failover group's separate read-only listener exists specifically for traffic that opts into `ApplicationIntent=ReadOnly` -- claims processing must never land there by accident.

## Step 4 — Re-run the drill and prove it now survives transparently

```sql
-- Connect to whichever server currently holds the secondary role
ALTER FAILOVER GROUP thornridge-sql-failover-group FAILOVER;
```

This time, the claims-processing app's write-error dashboard stays flat. The listener redirects every new connection to whichever server now holds the primary role, with no configuration change and no restart required on the app's part -- exactly what the failover group was built to provide back in Lesson 11, now actually working end to end.

## Step 5 — Fix the real root cause, not just the symptom

The connection string was the bug; the untested DR plan was the root cause. A quarterly tested-failover-drill schedule gets added to the `thornridge-automation` Automation Account from Lesson 13 -- a runbook that performs exactly this failover, verifies application writes succeed within five minutes, fails back, and logs the result, with a human reviewing the log every quarter rather than discovering the next configuration drift live during an actual regional incident.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Root cause: claims-processing-app's connection string had Server= hardcoded to thornridge-sql-server.database.windows.net instead of the failover group listener. Confirmed via az webapp config connection-string list, then fixed by pointing it at thornridge-sql-failover-group.database.windows.net with ApplicationIntent=ReadWrite explicit, redeployed, and re-ran the drill -- the app now survives a failover with zero reconfiguration. Added a quarterly tested-failover-drill runbook to thornridge-automation so this gap can't go untested again.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: Found and fixed the actual cause: the application was never pointed at the failover group's listener, so it didn't follow the automatic redirect when the database failed over. It's fixed, verified with a second drill, and we've scheduled recurring quarterly drills going forward so DR readiness gets tested continuously instead of assumed.
workplaceExplanation.executive: We found and fixed the real cause of today's incident -- a configuration gap that meant our claims system wasn't using the automatic failover protection we built. It's fixed and proven with a second test. More importantly, we're now testing this setup every quarter going forward, so we find gaps like this ourselves instead of during a real outage.

lessons.title: Connecting a Monitoring Dashboard to Azure SQL Metrics
lessons.summary: Wiring Azure SQL Database's own metrics -- DTU/vCore utilization, failed connections, and geo-replication lag on the secondary -- into an Azure Monitor workbook that IT leadership can check without asking you.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
Everything built so far on this project -- the migration, the security hardening, the failover group, the Query Store baseline, the maintenance runbooks, the CI/CD pipeline, even the connection-string fix from the last two lessons -- lives inside tools a DBA opens. IT leadership doesn't open Query Store or read DACPAC deployment logs. This video closes that gap by wiring `thornridge-sql-server` and `PolicyClaimsDB`'s own built-in metrics into an Azure Monitor workbook: DTU/vCore utilization on the primary, failed connection attempts, and the one number this project cares about most now -- geo-replication lag between the primary and the `thornridge-sql-failover-group` secondary.

This isn't a new monitoring system bolted on from outside. Azure SQL Database already emits every one of these metrics for free; the work here is choosing the right ones, setting thresholds that mean something for an insurance workload, and putting them somewhere a non-DBA can glance at during a Monday morning check-in instead of paging someone.
lessons.explainSimple:
Think about the dashboard in a car. The engine was always running, always making heat, using fuel, spinning at some speed -- but none of that was visible to the driver until someone put gauges on the dashboard: a speedometer, a fuel gauge, a temperature light. The engine didn't change. What changed is that the driver can now see, at a glance, whether everything is fine or whether something needs attention before it becomes a breakdown.

Azure SQL Database has been quietly tracking its own "engine numbers" the whole time -- how hard the database is working, how many connections are failing, how far behind the backup copy is. This video builds the dashboard. We're not changing how the database runs; we're putting gauges where people who aren't DBAs can actually see them.
lessons.explainProfessional:
Azure SQL Database surfaces its own telemetry through Azure Monitor automatically -- DTU or vCore percentage, data IO, log IO, connection counts and failures, and, for a geo-replicated database, replication lag on the secondary -- all without any agent to install. The work in this lesson is curation and presentation, not instrumentation: deciding which of the dozens of available metrics actually matter for Thornridge's workload, and building a workbook that reads as "is the policy and claims system healthy" rather than a wall of raw counters only a DBA can interpret.

We build this as an Azure Monitor workbook rather than standing up a separate Grafana instance, for a deliberate reason: the metrics already live in Azure Monitor, the workbook authors directly against that same Log Analytics workspace already created for diagnostic settings and auditing, and it ships inside the Azure portal where IT leadership already has a login -- no new tool, no new credential, no separate server to patch and secure. The three panels that matter most for this audience are DTU/vCore utilization (is the database approaching the ceiling of its current tier), failed connections (a leading indicator of either an application bug or, as we found two lessons ago, a connection string that isn't resolving the way it should), and replication lag seconds on the secondary (the number that tells us, before any failover drill, whether a real failover today would actually meet our recovery point objective). Each gets its own threshold band tuned to Thornridge's actual workload, not a generic default.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 — Confirm diagnostic settings are already feeding Log Analytics

This project's audit hardening in the earlier lessons already turned on Azure SQL Auditing and diagnostic logging. Confirm the same Log Analytics workspace also has the metrics category enabled, not just audit logs:

```
Azure Portal > thornridge-sql-server > PolicyClaimsDB > Diagnostic settings
  Name: policyclaimsdb-diagnostics
  Categories enabled:
    [x] SQLInsights
    [x] AutomaticTuning
    [x] Errors
    [x] DatabaseWaitStatistics
    [x] Timeouts
    [x] Blocks
    [x] Basic (includes DTU/vCore %, connections, failed connections)
  Destination: Log Analytics workspace -- thornridge-law
```

If `Basic` wasn't already checked from the earlier auditing lesson, enable it now -- it's the category that carries DTU/vCore percentage and connection counts, and it costs nothing extra since the workspace already exists.

## Step 2 — Confirm the failover group secondary reports its own lag metric

```
Azure Portal > thornridge-sql-failover-group > Replication
  Primary:    thornridge-sql-server (East US 2)
  Secondary:  thornridge-sql-server-secondary (Central US)
  Replication lag:  reported in seconds, visible per-database
```

This is the number lesson 16's failover drill made everyone care about. A healthy secondary should show lag in the low single-digit seconds under normal load; anything climbing steadily, rather than just spiking briefly under a batch job, is worth alerting on before it becomes a real recovery-time problem during an actual failover.

## Step 3 — Build the Azure Monitor workbook

```
Azure Portal > Monitor > Workbooks > New
Title: Thornridge PolicyClaimsDB Health

Panel 1 -- DTU/vCore Utilization
  Metric: dtu_consumption_percent (or cpu_percent on vCore-based tiers)
  Resource: PolicyClaimsDB
  Aggregation: Avg, Max
  Time range: last 24h, with a 7-day comparison overlay
  Threshold band: green < 70%, amber 70-85%, red > 85%

Panel 2 -- Failed Connections
  Metric: connection_failed
  Split by: client_ip (top 10)
  Threshold band: green < 5/hour, amber 5-20/hour, red > 20/hour
  Note: this is the exact signal that would have caught the bypassed
  connection string earlier -- a spike here after a deploy is now a
  known pattern to watch for, not just background noise

Panel 3 -- Geo-Replication Lag (secondary)
  Metric: replication_lag_seconds (from the failover group's secondary)
  Threshold band: green < 10s, amber 10-60s, red > 60s sustained

Panel 4 -- Active Connections vs. Limit
  Metric: connection_successful, overlaid against the tier's max
  connection limit, so a slow climb toward the ceiling is visible
  before it causes throttling
```

## Step 4 — Write the KQL queries behind each panel, not just the portal defaults

The portal's built-in metric charts are a starting point, but the workbook's real value is a query tuned to this workload:

```kql
// Failed connections, last 24h, grouped hourly
AzureDiagnostics
| where ResourceProvider == "MICROSOFT.SQL" and Category == "Errors"
| where Message has "Failed to connect"
| summarize FailedConnections = count() by bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
| order by TimeGenerated asc

// Replication lag trend on the secondary
AzureMetrics
| where ResourceId has "thornridge-sql-server-secondary"
| where MetricName == "replication_lag_seconds"
| summarize AvgLagSeconds = avg(Average) by bin(TimeGenerated, 15m)
| order by TimeGenerated asc
```

## Step 5 — Set alert rules on top of the same metrics, not just the dashboard

A dashboard nobody is watching at 2 a.m. doesn't help. Wire the two highest-value panels to action groups:

```
Alert rule 1: DTU/vCore > 85% for 15 minutes sustained
  Action group: thornridge-dba-oncall (email + Teams webhook)

Alert rule 2: Replication lag > 60 seconds sustained for 10 minutes
  Action group: thornridge-dba-oncall
  Severity: Sev 2 -- this is the metric that would have flagged, in
  advance, whether a real failover that day would hit its recovery
  point objective
```

## Step 6 — Pin the workbook where leadership actually looks

Publish the workbook, pin it to a shared Azure dashboard, and share the dashboard URL (view-only, via Azure RBAC reader role scoped to the resource group) with IT leadership directly -- not a screenshot emailed once, a live tile they can open themselves. Walk one person from leadership through it live for five minutes: what green looks like, what a single amber reading means versus a sustained one, and who gets paged if something turns red. A dashboard nobody was shown how to read gets ignored the same way an unexplained report does.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Enabled the Basic diagnostic category feeding thornridge-law, confirmed the failover group secondary reports replication lag in seconds, and built an Azure Monitor workbook with four panels: DTU/vCore utilization, failed connections (the same signal that would have caught the bypassed connection string), replication lag on the secondary, and active connections against the tier limit. Alert rules are wired on sustained DTU >85% and lag >60s, routed to the DBA on-call action group.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: Leadership now has a live dashboard showing database health, connection problems, and how far behind the backup database is running -- without needing to ask a DBA to pull a report. Alerts are set so the team gets paged on real problems automatically, not just when someone happens to look at the screen.
workplaceExplanation.executive: You can now check, yourself, whether the policy and claims database is healthy and whether our backup database is keeping up -- the same system that failed its first drill now has a live gauge on exactly the number that mattered in that drill. No report request needed; it's a dashboard you can open any time.

lessons.title: Presenting the Migrated, Secured, and Tested Database to Leadership
lessons.summary: The real presentation moment: walking IT and business leadership through the finished migration, including an honest account of the failed failover drill -- what happened, why it was a real and easy-to-miss gap, and the good news that a drill is exactly where it should have been caught.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
This is the moment the whole project has been building toward: a room with Thornridge's IT leadership and a couple of business stakeholders, looking at what actually got built -- the migration off the aging on-prem server, the security and auditing hardening, Query Store's performance baseline, the automated maintenance runbooks, CI/CD-deployed schema changes, and the monitoring dashboard from the last lesson. It also means walking into the room and talking, without flinching, about the failover drill two lessons ago that didn't work the first time.

The skill in this video isn't technical. It's explaining a real incident -- the connection string that bypassed `thornridge-sql-failover-group`'s listener -- honestly: what happened, why a reasonable, careful setup still missed it, and the genuinely good news underneath the bad news, which is that this was caught in a drill, on a Tuesday afternoon with no customers affected, instead of during a real outage. That is not a consolation prize. That is exactly what a tested failover process is supposed to do, and most companies never find out their failover is broken until the day it actually matters.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine your family installs a backup generator for the house, and then does a practice test: you flip the main breaker to simulate a blackout, and the generator doesn't kick on. You find out it's because an extension cord was plugged into the wrong outlet, not the special one wired to the generator circuit. That's annoying to discover! But think about the alternative: finding this out during a real blackout, in a storm, with the fridge full of food on the line.

That's exactly what happened here. The practice failover test found a real problem -- an app that wasn't plugged into the right "outlet" -- on a quiet afternoon with nothing actually at risk. It got fixed, and now there's a schedule to keep testing it. The whole point of running a drill is to find the broken extension cord before the storm, and that's exactly what happened.
lessons.explainProfessional:
The structure of this meeting matters as much as the content: lead with what's genuinely done and working, name the drill failure directly and specifically rather than glossing over it, and close by reframing "we failed a drill" as "the drill did its job." Skipping straight to the highlight reel erodes trust the moment someone asks about reliability; burying the incident in vague language ("we had some hiccups with failover") erodes trust just as fast once someone asks a follow-up question you can't answer specifically.

The honest version of the incident is specific: the application's connection string was pointed directly at `thornridge-sql-server.database.windows.net` instead of the failover group's listener endpoint, `thornridge-sql-failover-group.database.windows.net`. Under normal operation this is invisible -- both resolve to a working, reachable database, and the app runs identically either way. The gap only surfaces at the exact moment a failover happens: the failover group updates DNS to point the listener at the new primary, but a connection string hard-coded to the original server name has no reason to ever re-resolve, so the app keeps trying to reach a server that is now the demoted secondary. That is a genuinely easy mistake to make, because nothing about normal, day-to-day operation ever exposes it -- which is precisely the argument for why a recurring, tested drill schedule is now a permanent fixture of this environment rather than a one-time checkbox. The fix itself was a one-line connection string change; the real deliverable is the drill cadence that now exists so a gap like this never again waits for a real outage to be discovered.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 — Open with the finished architecture, plainly, before the incident

Start by reminding the room, briefly, where this started: a core policy and claims database that had run on the same on-premises SQL Server for over thirteen years, serving roughly 340,000 active policies and a claims team processing around 2,400 claims a day, which came within one more failed disk of a real outage back in Lesson 1. That's the baseline everything below gets measured against.

```
WHAT'S BUILT AND RUNNING TODAY:

  Migration:    On-prem SQL Server -> Azure Data Factory -> Azure SQL
                Database (thornridge-sql-server / PolicyClaimsDB)
  Security:     TDE at rest, Azure AD authentication, auditing to
                Log Analytics, least-privilege access reviewed
  HA/DR:        Active geo-replication + thornridge-sql-failover-group,
                auto-failover configured, secondary in a separate region
  Performance:  Query Store baseline captured and reviewed
  Automation:   PowerShell/Azure Automation maintenance runbooks
                (index maintenance, integrity checks, backup verification)
  CI/CD:        DACPAC-based schema deployment through a pull-request
                gated pipeline -- no more manual schema changes applied
                by hand against production
  Monitoring:   Azure Monitor workbook live now (last lesson), covering
                utilization, failed connections, and replication lag
```

Say this part plainly and without hedging -- it's real, it's in production, and it's the majority of the project.

## Step 2 — Name the incident directly, with the specific mechanism

```
"During our scheduled failover drill, the failover didn't complete
cleanly on the application side. Here's exactly what happened: the
application's connection string pointed directly at the primary
server's own name instead of the failover group's listener endpoint.
Under normal operation, both work identically -- the problem only
shows up at the moment of an actual failover, which is exactly why a
drill, and not day-to-day use, is what caught it."
```

## Step 3 — Explain why this was a real, easy-to-miss gap -- not a careless mistake

```
"The failover group's listener endpoint and the primary server's own
endpoint both resolve to a working database on a normal day. There was
no outage, no error, no symptom at all until the one moment that
matters -- a failover -- and that moment doesn't happen often enough
for this kind of gap to surface on its own. This is a known, common
failure pattern in Azure SQL failover group setups, not a one-off
oversight specific to this build."
```

## Step 4 — State the good news plainly, and mean it

```
"The reason this matters less than it sounds is that it was caught in
a drill. Nobody's claims processing was affected, nobody's policy data
was at risk, and nothing about the business day was disrupted. This is
literally what a failover drill exists to do -- find the gap on a
Tuesday afternoon with nothing at stake, instead of during a real
incident with customers waiting. A company that never drills its
failover doesn't have a system that works -- it has a system that
hasn't been tested yet."
```

## Step 5 — Show what's in place now as a direct result

```
FIX:      Connection string updated to the failover group listener
          endpoint (thornridge-sql-failover-group.database.windows.net)
          across every application and service connecting to
          PolicyClaimsDB
VERIFIED: A second drill, after the fix, completed a clean failover
          with the application reconnecting automatically
GOING FORWARD: A recurring, scheduled failover drill -- not a one-time
          test -- is now a standing item on the DBA calendar, so any
          future gap, in this connection string or a new one introduced
          by a later change, gets caught the same way this one was
```

## Step 6 — Rehearse the question that will come up

```
Q: "How do we know there isn't another hidden gap like this one
    somewhere else?"
A: "We don't know that with certainty -- nobody legitimately can. What
    we do know is that we now have a recurring drill schedule whose
    entire purpose is finding exactly this kind of gap before it
    matters, instead of hoping none exists. That's the actual answer
    to this question, not a guarantee that nothing will ever be found."
```

## Step 7 — Close by naming what this meeting is actually for

End by asking for explicit sign-off that the migration is considered production-ready and that the recurring drill cadence is understood and supported by leadership -- including the fact that a future drill might surface another gap, and that this is the system working as intended, not a sign something is wrong.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Presented the completed build to leadership: migration, security hardening, geo-replication and failover group, Query Store baseline, automation runbooks, CI/CD, and the monitoring workbook. Walked through the failover drill incident with the exact mechanism -- connection string pointed at the primary server name instead of the failover group listener -- and the fix and verification that followed. Framed the drill finding the gap as the drill succeeding, not the system failing.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: Got leadership sign-off on the finished migration in one meeting, including an honest accounting of the one real issue the project hit. Nobody left the room thinking anything was hidden, and everyone understood why the drill schedule going forward is a permanent fixture, not a one-time task that's now checked off.
workplaceExplanation.executive: The migration is done, secured, and tested. We hit one real issue during a practice failover -- an application wasn't pointed at the right failover address -- and found it on a quiet afternoon instead of during an actual outage, which is exactly what that drill was for. It's fixed, verified with a second successful drill, and we now test this on a recurring schedule so we're not relying on luck to catch the next one.

lessons.title: Writing the Handoff Docs: Runbooks, DR Plan, and a Failover Checklist
lessons.summary: Writing the real documents that let someone else run this system without you: a step-by-step DR failover runbook with a listener-endpoint checklist item, a security/access reference, and a plain-prose lineage description of the whole architecture.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
A migration that only the person who built it can operate isn't actually finished -- it's a dependency on one person. This video writes the three documents that let any on-call DBA, not just you, run this system: a step-by-step DR failover runbook that includes, as its own explicit checklist item, verifying every connected application uses the failover group's listener endpoint; a security and access reference covering Azure AD authentication, TDE, and auditing; and a plain-prose description of the system's lineage -- on-prem SQL Server through the ADF migration, into the geo-replicated Azure SQL pair, deployed through CI/CD, watched by the monitoring workbook.

The failover checklist item is the direct, permanent artifact of the incident from the last two lessons. It exists specifically so that the exact gap that caused the first drill to fail -- an application quietly pointed at the wrong endpoint -- gets checked for, by name, every single time, instead of depending on anyone remembering that it happened once.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine you're the only person in your family who knows how to work the water shutoff valve during an emergency -- which pipe, which direction to turn it, how long it takes. That's useful right up until the day you're out of town and the basement starts flooding. A good handoff means writing it down clearly enough that anyone in the family could follow the steps and shut off the water correctly, even if you're not there to explain it.

This video writes down exactly that, for the database: the steps to follow if the main system goes down, who's allowed to access what and why, and a plain description of how all the pieces fit together -- written clearly enough that someone who wasn't in any of the last eighteen videos could still pick it up and run it correctly.
lessons.explainProfessional:
A DR runbook that exists only as tribal knowledge in one DBA's head is, functionally, a single point of failure identical in shape to the hardware failure this whole migration was meant to eliminate. The three documents built here serve distinct audiences and distinct failure modes: the failover runbook is written for whoever is on call during an actual incident, under pressure, at 2 a.m., and needs to execute correct steps in order without needing to reason from first principles; the security and access reference is written for an auditor or a new team member who needs to understand what's enforced and why, not how to operate it; and the lineage description is written for anyone -- technical or not -- who needs to understand the shape of the whole system without reading a single line of T-SQL or PowerShell.

The runbook's pre-failover checklist is the most load-bearing paragraph in this entire series. It exists because the connection-string gap was real, specific, and silent under normal operation -- which means the only reliable defense against it recurring, in this app or the next one connected to this database, is a checklist line that gets read and actively verified every single time a failover is executed or drilled, not a one-time fix trusted to hold forever. Writing "verify every connected application's connection string resolves through thornridge-sql-failover-group.database.windows.net, not the primary server's own name" as its own numbered, unskippable step is what turns one incident into a permanent process improvement instead of a story people eventually stop telling.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 — Write the DR failover runbook as a numbered, executable sequence

This project started because Thornridge's recovery depended on one person: Carl Dunmore, the on-prem DBA whose own discipline about log backups was the only reason Lesson 1's near-miss didn't cost real data. The runbook below exists so recovery never again depends on one person's memory.

```
THORNRIDGE POLICYCLAIMSDB -- DR FAILOVER RUNBOOK

WHEN TO USE: Primary region (East US 2) outage affecting
thornridge-sql-server, confirmed via the Azure Monitor workbook
showing sustained connection failures AND an Azure Service Health
alert for the East US 2 region -- not on a single alert alone.

PRE-FAILOVER CHECKLIST (complete before triggering failover):
  [ ] Confirm this is a genuine regional/primary outage, not a
      transient blip -- check Azure Service Health first
  [ ] Confirm replication lag on the secondary was under 60 seconds
      at last healthy reading (check the monitoring workbook) --
      this bounds expected data loss
  [ ] *** Verify every connected application's connection string
      resolves through thornridge-sql-failover-group.database.
      windows.net -- NOT thornridge-sql-server.database.windows.net
      directly. This is the exact gap that caused the first drill
      to fail. Check the claims-portal, policy-admin, and reporting
      service configs by name, every time. ***
  [ ] Notify the on-call lead and open an incident ticket

FAILOVER STEPS:
  1. If auto-failover hasn't already triggered (grace period 1 hour),
     initiate manually: Azure Portal > thornridge-sql-failover-group
     > Failover, or via PowerShell:
       Switch-AzSqlDatabaseFailoverGroup -ResourceGroupName "rg-thornridge-sql-prod" `
         -ServerName "thornridge-sql-server-secondary" `
         -FailoverGroupName "thornridge-sql-failover-group"
  2. Confirm the listener now reports the former secondary as primary
     (Get-AzSqlDatabaseFailoverGroup against the same names)
  3. Confirm applications reconnect within 5 minutes -- if any do not,
     that application's connection string is the first thing to check
  4. Monitor the workbook for failed connections and utilization on
     the new primary for the next 30 minutes
  5. Update the incident ticket with the failover timestamp and
     confirmed recovery time

POST-FAILOVER:
  [ ] Once the original region recovers, do NOT fail back
      automatically -- schedule failback during a low-traffic window
      and repeat the pre-failover checklist in reverse
  [ ] Log the drill or incident in the DR test log (Step 5 below)
```

## Step 2 — Write the security and access reference

```
THORNRIDGE POLICYCLAIMSDB -- SECURITY & ACCESS REFERENCE

Authentication: Azure AD only -- SQL authentication is disabled at
  the server level. Every human and service account authenticates
  through Azure AD, no exceptions.

Encryption: TDE enabled at rest on both primary and secondary. TLS
  enforced in transit (minimum version set at the server level).

Auditing: Azure SQL Auditing enabled, writing to the thornridge-law
  Log Analytics workspace.

Access model: Role-based, least privilege. Application service
  principals hold only the permissions their function requires
  (claims-portal-svc: read/write on claims schema only; reporting-svc:
  read-only on reporting views). No application connects as owner.

Who can trigger a manual failover: DBA on-call and the DBA lead only
-- deliberately short, since a failover is a significant action.
```

## Step 3 — Write the lineage/architecture description in plain prose

```
THORNRIDGE POLICYCLAIMSDB -- HOW IT'S PUT TOGETHER

The system started as an on-premises SQL Server instance running the
policy and claims database. That data was migrated using Azure Data
Factory into a new Azure SQL Database -- thornridge-sql-server,
database PolicyClaimsDB.

From there, two protections were added: encryption at rest with
Azure AD-only authentication and full auditing, and a geo-replicated
secondary in a separate Azure region joined under an auto-failover
group -- thornridge-sql-failover-group -- so a regional outage can be
survived by redirecting traffic automatically.

Schema changes no longer happen by connecting directly to production
and running a script -- they go through a DACPAC-based CI/CD pipeline.
Maintenance runs on its own schedule through PowerShell inside Azure
Automation. The whole system is watched through the Azure Monitor
workbook, with alerts wired to the DBA on-call group.

The one real incident this project surfaced -- a failover drill that
didn't complete cleanly because an application's connection string
pointed at the primary server directly instead of the failover
group's listener -- is now a permanent checklist item, and the drill
itself runs on a recurring schedule rather than as a one-time test.
```

## Step 4 — Attach a DR test log template, not just a one-time result

```
DR TEST LOG
Date        Type         Result              Notes
----------  -----------  ------------------  ----------------------
[date 1]    Drill        FAILED              App connection strings
                                              bypassed listener
[date 2]    Drill        PASSED              Fix verified, all apps
                                              reconnected < 5 min
[next date] Drill        (scheduled)         Recurring quarterly
```

This log turns "we tested it once" into a real, auditable practice -- the first thing to show an auditor or a new DBA who asks "how do we know this works."

## Step 5 — Walk one other person through all three documents, live

Spend thirty minutes walking the on-call DBA through the runbook, line by line, including the listener-endpoint checklist item, and have them repeat back why it exists. A document nobody's been walked through gets skipped under exactly the pressure a real failover happens under.

## Step 6 — Store all three where the next on-call DBA will actually find them

Commit the runbook, security reference, and lineage description to the team's shared ops wiki -- not a personal OneNote -- and link the DR test log from the same page. Cross-link the runbook from the monitoring workbook's description field, so anyone responding to an alert is one click from the steps to follow.

lessons.title: Wrap-Up: What Changed, and What's Still Manual
lessons.summary: The honest closing assessment of the Thornridge Insurance build -- what's genuinely solved, and what still depends on a human remembering to do it, including a real decommission task nobody has done yet.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
This is the last video in the series, and like the project it closes out, it isn't a highlight reel. Over nineteen lessons, Thornridge Insurance's policy and claims database went from an aging, at-risk on-premises SQL Server box to a secured, geo-replicated, tested, automated, CI/CD-deployed Azure SQL Database, monitored on a live dashboard and documented well enough for someone else to run it. That part is real, it's in production, and it's genuinely done.

What this video does instead of celebrating is the harder, more useful thing: naming exactly what's still manual, still imperfect, or still a human-dependent process, so whoever maintains this platform next -- possibly you, months from now -- isn't caught off guard by a limitation that was always there but never said out loud.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine you spent months renovating an old house -- new wiring, a new roof, a generator for power outages, smoke detectors in every room. It's genuinely much safer and better than before. But a good contractor doesn't just hand over the keys and say "it's perfect, goodbye" -- they say "the smoke detectors still need their batteries checked twice a year, the old shed out back still needs to be torn down, and that generator is only as good as the last time someone tested it." That honesty is what keeps the house actually safe to live in, instead of someone discovering a gap the hard way later.

That's this whole video: being straight about what's genuinely solid in what we built for Thornridge, and what still needs a person checking in on it.
lessons.explainProfessional:
A credible project retrospective does two things most victory-lap wrap-ups skip: it states the real architecture plainly enough that someone who missed the first nineteen videos could still understand what's running, and it enumerates the actual gaps with the same specificity the earlier lessons used for the connection-string incident -- not "there's room for improvement," but named, concrete limitations with an owner and a reason. For Thornridge, three are worth stating without softening.

First, the recurring failover drill schedule set up two lessons ago is a calendar entry and a runbook, not an automated system -- a human still has to actually run it on schedule, and a drill that quietly stops happening because nobody got around to it this quarter provides zero protection despite looking, on paper, like a solved problem. Second, the original on-premises SQL Server instance technically still exists; it was the migration source, not something torn down the moment the cutover succeeded, and a formal decommission -- confirming no lingering application or report still points at it, then powering it down and removing it from the environment -- is a real, scoped task that has not happened yet. Third, the Query Store performance baseline captured earlier in this project is a snapshot of a workload at one point in time, not a permanent truth; as Thornridge's claims volume grows or the application changes, that baseline needs periodic re-capture, or "performance regression" alerts will eventually be measured against a baseline that no longer reflects how the system is actually used. Naming these isn't an admission of failure -- overselling a system's completeness to a stakeholder is itself a trust problem, the same category of problem the connection-string incident already taught this room to take seriously. The honest version of "done" is "this solved the specific, real problem we scoped, these are its real edges, and here's what a future phase would need to address them."
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 — State the finished architecture in one pass, end to end

```
SOURCE:         On-premises SQL Server (policy and claims database)
MIGRATION:      Azure Data Factory, one-time cutover
PRIMARY:        thornridge-sql-server / PolicyClaimsDB (East US 2)
HA/DR:          Active geo-replication + thornridge-sql-failover-group,
                secondary in Central US, auto-failover configured
SECURITY:       TDE at rest, Azure AD-only auth, auditing to
                Log Analytics, least-privilege service accounts
PERFORMANCE:    Query Store baseline captured and reviewed
AUTOMATION:     PowerShell/Azure Automation runbooks for index
                maintenance, integrity checks, backup verification
CI/CD:          DACPAC-based schema deployment, pull-request gated
MONITORING:     Azure Monitor workbook -- utilization, failed
                connections, replication lag -- with alerting
DOCUMENTATION:  DR failover runbook (with the listener-endpoint
                checklist), security reference, lineage description
INCIDENT FOUND & FIXED: A failover drill caught an application
                connection string bypassing the failover group
                listener. Fixed, re-verified, now a permanent
                checklist item and a recurring drill schedule.
```

Every box in that chain was built, tested, and is now running in production -- that's the real, defensible claim this project gets to make.

## Step 2 — Name what's still manual, specifically

```
GAP 1: The failover drill schedule still depends on a human running it.
  The runbook and the calendar entry exist, but nothing forces the
  quarterly drill to actually happen. A drill that quietly stops
  running provides the same amount of real protection as no drill at
  all, while still looking, on paper, like a solved problem. This is
  a process risk, not a technology gap -- no script fixes "someone
  has to remember to do this."

GAP 2: The original on-premises SQL Server has not been decommissioned.
  The same thirteen-plus-year-old box from Lesson 1 -- the one that
  nearly took down claims processing over a second failed disk -- was
  the migration source, and cutover succeeding didn't include tearing
  it down. It's still sitting there, still a server someone
  has to patch, secure, and pay for, and still a risk if any report or
  legacy integration nobody remembers about is still quietly pointed
  at it instead of PolicyClaimsDB. Decommissioning it is a real,
  scoped task -- confirm nothing still depends on it, then retire it --
  that simply hasn't been done yet.

GAP 3: The Query Store performance baseline will age.
  It's a snapshot of the workload at the time it was captured, not a
  permanent definition of "normal." As claims volume grows or the
  application changes, performance comparisons against this baseline
  will drift out of relevance unless someone deliberately re-captures
  it on a periodic basis.
```

## Step 3 — Write the honest one-paragraph summary for whoever reads this next

```
"This project replaced an aging, single-point-of-failure on-premises
database with a secured, geo-replicated, tested, and monitored Azure
SQL Database, deployed through CI/CD and documented well enough for
someone else to operate. It found and fixed a real failover gap along
the way. It did not automate the drill schedule itself, decommission
the original on-premises server, or build a process for re-baselining
performance as the workload grows -- those are real, named gaps for a
future phase, not oversights we're pretending don't exist."
```

## Step 4 — Leave a short, prioritized list for "if there's a phase two"

```
1. Decommission the original on-premises SQL Server -- confirm no
   lingering dependency, then retire it. Closes Gap 2, and removes a
   real ongoing cost and risk, not just a tidiness issue.
2. Add a calendar-enforced reminder or lightweight automation around
   the quarterly failover drill, so it can't quietly lapse. Closes
   Gap 1 -- lower technical lift, meaningful risk reduction.
3. Schedule a periodic Query Store re-baseline (e.g., twice a year, or
   after any major application change) as a standing maintenance task.
   Closes Gap 3.
```

## Step 5 — Close the series the way it should close: honestly, not triumphantly

This is the last video of twenty. Resist the pull to end on an unqualified victory lap. The real ending is: a genuinely dangerous single point of failure -- an aging on-premises server with no tested recovery plan -- is gone, replaced by something secured, geo-replicated, automated, and actually drilled. One real gap was found and fixed along the way, which is a better outcome than a project that never finds out its gaps exist. And three honest, specific limitations remain, named and handed off instead of hidden. That's a finished project, not a perfect one -- and that distinction is the whole point of this series.
